I have a Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) preference: I do not want resuscitation performed during a medical emergency while care is being delivered. Call 000 and notify my support people.

I am diabetic (Type 2) and follow a diabetic diet. I have Barrett’s oesophagus and cannot eat lettuce, bananas, or tomatoes. I prefer small portions.

I have allergies to: morphine, Acupan, Dacogridic, and Ghatran.

I have hearing issues; please speak clearly and loudly, and check my understanding.

I live with osteoarthritis pain (baseline 5/10; up to 10/10 with flares). Heat worsens my pain.

I have lymphedema and occasional skin ulcers; monitor skin integrity and avoid skin breaks.

I have atrial fibrillation and hypertension; monitor for shortness of breath and dizziness.

I have limited mobility and use a walker; I am at increased falls risk, especially in the bathroom and during transfers.

I have a Live Life personal alarm (subscription ~$75/year) and will use it in emergencies.

I prefer female workers for showering support.

I have a cat; please be mindful of a potential trip hazard on entry.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 2 September 2025

Preferred Name: Lydia

Full Name: Lydia Mae Goodwin

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I participated in this assessment and plan with Thomas (care partner/home care representative). I make my own decisions. Claudette and Craig hold my Enduring Power of Attorney. My GP is Dr Dina Halawani (HAFI Medical Centre). These people may be contacted to support my care, with my consent.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I was born in Balclutha, New Zealand. I identify as Anglican but I am not currently attending services.

My values include family, good manners/morals, my independence, and peace in the world.

I do not have any specific cultural match preferences for workers.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer female workers for showering support.

Please speak clearly and loudly due to my hearing issues, and confirm my understanding.

On bad days (pain or digestive issues), I prefer to be left alone and have privacy; please check what I want on the day.

Service times agreed: Personal Care Monday/Wednesday/Friday at 9:00–10:00; Domestic Assistance Mondays 10:00–11:00; Transport/Social Support every second Tuesday 9:00–12:00. Home maintenance twice per year (3 hours each).

Please do not schedule cleaning before the shower on Mondays; 10:00 a.m. is suitable after my 9:00 a.m. shower.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination

My Preferred Support People

Craig – family support and emergency contact; Enduring Power of Attorney.

Claudette – family support; Enduring Power of Attorney.

Claudette’s mum – supportive.

My sisters and close friends (including friends in New Zealand, such as Sarah) are important to me.

Informal Supports

My family helps me as needed. I also use a personal alarm (Live Life) for emergencies.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I was raised in care homes after my father died when I was four. I met my husband at 17 and married in November 1962. I worked in retail, factory work, hospitals, and later in a woollen factory before retiring. I moved from New Zealand to Australia on 1 April (arriving 2 April) two years before this assessment.

I have one child and two grandchildren. I later learned I am one of 11 siblings and came to know some siblings in adulthood.

Interests

I enjoy reading, crosswords, and playing word games on the computer. I like country music and previously belonged to a country music club. I also participate online in genealogy groups. I have one cat.

My Medical Information

Medical History:

Type 2 diabetes; lymphedema; osteoarthritis; hypercholesterolemia; hypertension; atrial fibrillation; Barrett’s oesophagus (dietary restrictions noted).

Pain: constant osteoarthritis pain (average 5/10; up to 10/10 during flares). Heat worsens my pain.

Skin: occasional ulcers; use of emollients (DMEs); no current wound dressings.

Cognition: no concerns raised in assessment.

Allergies: morphine, Acupan, Dacogridic, Ghatran.

Medication:

I take regular medications supplied in a Webstar pack from my medical centre’s in-house pharmacy. I take osteoarthritis pain tablets once daily, and up to three times daily during flares. I self-manage my medicines and do not require assistance. I see a diabetes educator as needed.

Mobility and Equipment:

I have limited mobility and primarily use a walker frame. I have walking sticks (used only when a walker won’t fit), a wheelchair, crutches, a medical chair, a shower chair, handrails in the bathroom, and a front ramp. I do not use a raised toilet seat because my toilet is higher-set. I can get in/out of a car if it is not too high. I wear full dentures.

GP / Pharmacy:

GP: Dr Dina Halawani, HAFI Medical Centre.

Pharmacy: HAFI Medical Centre in-house pharmacy (provides Webstar packs).

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

CALD: No – I speak English and do not require an interpreter.

Living with disability (mobility): Yes – limited mobility; walker dependent; bathroom and transfer risks.

Mental health (low mood/isolation risk): I prefer to be left alone on bad days; there is some risk of social withdrawal during pain or digestive flares.

Specific Risks

  • Falls risk related to limited mobility, osteoarthritis pain, and bathroom transfers.
  • Skin integrity risk due to lymphedema and occasional ulcers.
  • Cardiac/respiratory symptoms related to atrial fibrillation and hypertension.
  • Communication risk due to hearing issues – need clear, loud, and paced communication.
  • Nutritional risk if dietary restrictions are not followed (diabetes and Barrett’s oesophagus).
  • Heat exacerbates pain, increasing functional limitation on hot days.
  • Emergency preparedness: I rely on my personal alarm and family; I do not have a formal emergency kit.
  • Trip hazard on entry due to my cat and general home environment.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

If I do not respond at a scheduled visit, please follow my safety plan: knock and call out, phone me and my nominated support people, and if concerned for my safety, call 000. I use a Live Life personal alarm and will activate it if needed.

During any medical emergency while care is being provided: do not perform resuscitation (DNR); call 000 and notify Craig and Claudette as my support people/EPOA.

Primary family support: Craig (family, EPOA) and Claudette (family, EPOA). Contact details will be provided to the care provider and attached to my file.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I have limited mobility, lymphedema, and occasional skin ulcers. I prefer a female worker. Falls risk in the bathroom is present.

How will we do this? (Tasks): A female Salveo support worker will assist with showering, including washing my back and hair, setting up my shower chair, checking water temperature, drying thoroughly (especially skin folds), and documenting skin checks each visit.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Personal Care worker and me. When will it be done?: 1 hour, Monday/Wednesday/Friday at 9–10 a.m., weekly for 12 weeks. How much will it be cost?: Personal Care $85/hour; 3 hours/week x 4 weeks = $1,020/month (Independence Support).

Service Category: Clinical Care / Independence Support / Everyday Living

GOAL 2 Goal: I will keep my home clean and manageable so I do not need to stand for long periods and my bathroom and linens are fresh each week for the next 3 months.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Standing increases my pain. I need help with vacuuming, mopping, changing bed sheets, and bathroom cleaning.

How will we do this? (Tasks): After my Monday shower, the worker will vacuum/mop high-traffic areas, clean the bathroom, and change my bed sheets. Tasks will be rotated if time is limited.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Domestic Assistance worker and me. When will it be done?: 1 hour every Monday 10–11 a.m., weekly for 12 weeks. How much will it be cost?: Domestic Assistance $85/hour; 1 hour/week x 4 weeks = $340/month (Everyday Living).

Service Category: Clinical Care / Independence Support / Everyday Living

GOAL 3 Goal: Every second Tuesday, I will go to Karingal to pick up my magazines, do light shopping, and have a coffee (9 a.m.–12 p.m.) to maintain my independence and enjoyment of community life over the next 3 months (aim: at least 5 outings).

Abilities and considerations (risks): I use a walker, have hearing issues, and may tire; I prefer a worker to stay with me for safety and company.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo will provide door-to-door transport, accompany me with my walker, assist with shopping, and allow time for a coffee. Rest breaks will be taken as needed.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Social Support/Transport worker and me. When will it be done?: 3 hours fortnightly (Tuesdays 9 a.m.–12 p.m.) for 12 weeks. How much will it be cost?: Social Support/Transport $85/hour; ~6 hours/month = $510/month, plus $1.40/km for mileage (Everyday Living).

Service Category: Clinical Care / Independence Support / Everyday Living

GOAL 4 Goal: I will maintain my foot health (hammer toes and other foot issues) to prevent ulcers and falls by completing podiatry visits as scheduled (target 2 sessions this quarter).

Abilities and considerations (risks): Diabetes and lymphedema increase skin and ulcer risk; I have foot deformities and need regular podiatry.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo will arrange allied health podiatry to trim nails, reduce callus/corns as required, assess footwear, and update my foot care plan. Workers will observe and report any foot skin changes.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Allied Health (Podiatry) and me. When will it be done?: 1-hour sessions, approximately every 6 weeks (2 sessions in 12 weeks). How much will it be cost?: Allied Health Therapist (Podiatry) $180/hour; average ~$120/month (2 sessions/quarter = $360/quarter). Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded).

Service Category: Clinical Care / Independence Support / Everyday Living

GOAL 5 Goal: I will complete an Occupational Therapy home safety and equipment assessment to confirm my equipment is optimal and reduce falls risk this quarter.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I already use a walker, shower chair, and handrails; I have bathroom and transfer risks.

How will we do this? (Tasks): A Salveo OT will conduct a 2-hour IAT-aligned assessment, review transfers and bathroom setup, and provide recommendations (e.g., layout, technique, minor AT). Any changes will be explained and, if agreed, implemented.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Allied Health Therapist (OT), Care Partner, and me. When will it be done?: One 2-hour assessment within 12 weeks. How much will it be cost?: $180/hour x 2 hours = $360 (one-off this quarter). Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded).

Service Category: Clinical Care / Independence Support / Everyday Living

GOAL 6 Goal: I will keep my home safe and maintained (gutters, windows, and minor repairs like loose nails/boards) to reduce trip hazards and water ingress, with seasonal work scheduled over the year.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Outdoor tasks are unsafe for me due to mobility and balance limitations.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo will book Light Home & Gardening Maintenance for 3 hours twice per year. Tasks will include gutter clearing, window cleaning, and minor safety fixes. If due this quarter, one visit will be completed.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Home & Garden Maintenance team and me. When will it be done?: 3 hours twice per year (schedule as seasonally due). How much will it be cost?: $85/hour; 6 hours/year = $510/year (~$42.50/month; ~$127.50/quarter) (Everyday Living).

Summary 
The meeting was an assessment interview between Thomas (a representative from Salveo Care), Ian (an elderly client), and Darryl (Ian's son). The purpose was to set up home care services for Ian under a government-funded package. 
Thomas collected Ian's personal information including Medicare and pension card details. Ian shared his difficult situation caring for his wife who has Alzheimer's and is now in permanent care. Ian expressed deep emotional distress about this situation, stating he would "give every cent away to gethiswife back." 
Ian's health issues were discussed in detail. He suffers from emphysema, which severely limits his mobility and energy levels. He can only walk about 10 meters before needing to rest. Ian also has a history of prostate cancer (stage 3-4), depression, and a brain aneurysm that doctors determined was too risky to operate on given his age. He was recently hospitalized in a mental health ward after a suicide attempt. 
Family dynamics were a significant topic. Ian has three children, but there's conflict between Darryl and his other two children (Paul and Laura). Ian expressed that Paul and Laura have "broken his heart" by distancing themselves, while Darryl has been extremely supportive, helping with pension arrangements, meal deliveries, and other assistance. 
Thomas worked with Ian and Darryl to establish a care plan within the constraints of Ian's Level 2 package budget (approximately $40,000 annually). They prioritized services including: 
•	Social support/companionship (2.5 hours weekly) 
•	Light and Easy meal deliveries (fortnightly) 
•	Monthly gardening/lawn mowing (1 hour) 
They discussed the need for a personal alarm system, with Ian preferring a pendant-style alarm ($567 one-off payment) rather than a smartwatch. Thomas mentioned that an Occupational Therapy assessment would be needed to justify purchasing mobility equipment like a wheelchair or walker. 
Thomas emphasized that Ian is "the boss" of his own care plan and cannot be forced to use services or follow recommendations. He also noted that getting Ian's package upgraded to Level 3 or 4 would be a priority to increase the available budget. 
The meeting concluded with scheduling services to begin the following week (starting on the 25th) and explaining the cancellation policy and complaint procedures.

Family Dynamics and Support System ‎ 00:27:52
Ian discussed his family situation, expressing distress about two of his children (Paul and Laura) who have distanced themselves. Ian explained that Paul and Laura seem resentful of Darryl's involvement, believing "he just wants to be the smart arse and be in charge," while Ian insisted "I'm controlling that." Thomas empathized, sharing that he feels he "owes" his parents support after all they gave him growing up. 
Health Assessment and Medical History ‎ 00:35:45
Darryl reported that Ian spent three weeks in a mental health ward about six months ago after a suicide attempt. Ian has diagnosed depression, had cancer removed about two years ago, received radiation for prostate cancer (stage 3-4) around 2007, and has a brain aneurysm that doctors won't operate on due to his age. Ian was diagnosed with emphysema shortly after his prostate cancer treatment, which has severely limited his energy and breathing capacity. Ian described his mobility challenges: "I just run out of energy so easily" and "anything physical, I'm incapable of." 
Current Lifestyle and Daily Activities ‎ 00:43:48
Ian shared that he used to enjoy playing tennis but can no longer do so. He mentioned that he enjoys taking his dog Rambo for walks (though this is now difficult), playing an "amusement machine," and occasionally going to the pokies (gambling) where he limits himself to $20. Ian described a good day as one where "I get up and I can breathe good, from the moment I get up," while a bad day is when he wakes up "short of energy" and knows he "can't do virtually anything." Ian mentioned he watches TV but "can't seem to get interested" in it anymore. 
Life History and Personal Background ‎ 00:47:02
Ian shared limited details about his childhood, mentioning he "never even wanted to go to school" and that "something terrible happened" when he was 4-5 years old that he can't recall. He has two brothers and three sisters and grew up near the zoo in Melbourne. Ian worked at a malt house in Collingwood when he was younger, and later owned a laundromat in Noble Park for about 20 years, which he sold only 1.5 years ago. He has three children and five grandchildren. 
Care Needs Assessment ‎ 01:25:06
Thomas assessed Ian's mobility, noting he requires assistance but doesn't currently use his recommended four-wheel walker because he finds it exhausting: "I'm exposing my energy using it all the time." Ian has fallen recently, describing one incident where he "went backwards and then fucking landed on the arse." The assessment revealed Ian has handrails in the toilet, bathroom, shower, and back door, but no shower chair, raised toilet seat, or bed transfer pole. Ian doesn't require assistance with personal care, oral care, or toileting, but does need help with meals through Light and Easy deliveries. 
Budget Planning and Service Prioritization ‎ 01:20:06
Thomas worked with Ian and Darryl to establish a care plan within the constraints of Ian's Level 2 package budget (approximately $40,000 annually). After accounting for provider charges, they had about $40,000 to spend on services for the year. They prioritized: 
•	Social support/companionship (2.5 hours weekly, scheduled for Wednesdays from 12:00-2:30) 
•	Light and Easy meal deliveries (fortnightly, $66 per month) 
•	Monthly gardening/lawn mowing (1 hour) 
Thomas emphasized that getting Ian's package upgraded to Level 3 or 4 would be a priority to increase the available budget. 
Equipment Needs and Personal Alarm Options ‎ 00:16:52
Thomas discussed personal alarm options with Ian and Darryl. They compared a smartwatch-style alarm ($600 upfront plus $40/month) with a pendant-style alarm ($567 one-off payment with no monthly fee). Ian preferred the pendant option: "I'd prefer it around the neck" because he could put it on in the morning with his medications. Thomas mentioned that an Occupational Therapy assessment would be needed to justify purchasing mobility equipment like a wheelchair or walker, but they decided to postpone this assessment since Ian might be moving to Darryl's house soon. 
Service Scheduling and Conclusion ‎ 01:37:34
They scheduled the social support for Wednesdays from 12:00-2:30, with no preference for gender or age of the support worker. Thomas explained the cancellation policy (24 hours notice required) and complaint procedures, noting that all complaints go directly to Archie, the CEO. Thomas provided contact information for Salveo Care and mentioned that services would begin the following week (starting on the 25th). He emphasized that Ian is "the boss" of his own care plan and cannot be forced to use services or follow recommendations.

risks.description: Recent falls including a backward fall causing a leg cut; very limited endurance; does not use recommended walker.
Diagnosed depression; suicide attempt ~6 months ago with 3-week admission to a mental health ward; ongoing grief about wife.
Severe emphysema; becomes breathless easily; can walk ~10 meters before resting; reports difficulty breathing especially after heater on overnight.
Lives alone; wife in care; estranged from two children; low interest in activities and TV.
Still drives despite severe breathlessness and fatigue.
Low body weight (~50 kg); relies on meal delivery for regular nutrition.

medical.pharmacy: Chemist Warehouse, 415 Springvale Road, Forest Hill (may change to Croydon when moving)
medical.medications: Uses a Webster pack; multiple daily medications; uses an inhaler/puffer morning and night (specific meds not listed).

support.secondaryContact: Paul and Laura (adult children) – limited/estranged contact
support.livingArrangement: Lives alone at home; wife in permanent residential aged care; considering moving in with son (Darryl). Has a dog (Rambo).

I smoke and I sometimes leave heating on overnight, which affects my breathing. This increases my respiratory risk.

I live with a small dog (Rambo) which may present a trip hazard when I am short of breath.

I continue to drive but fatigue and breathlessness can affect my capacity.

I prefer a pendant-style personal alarm and have agreed to wear it daily once supplied.

I do not have a preference for worker gender, age, or cultural background.

My Preferred Support People

My preferred contact and advocate is my son Darryl.

Other important people in my life include my wife (in permanent aged care), friends and neighbours: Bruce and Anne (across the road), Josie, Glenn and Cherry, Terri, Kevin, Brendan, Bernie, and Robin.

Informal Supports

Darryl assists me with many things including pension arrangements, coordinating meal deliveries, and general support. Friends and neighbours check in on me at times.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I grew up in Melbourne near the zoo with two brothers and three sisters. I worked at a malt house in Collingwood (James Hood & Company) as a young man and later owned a laundromat in Noble Park for around 20 years, which I sold about 1.5 years ago. I have three children and five grandchildren. I am deeply devoted to my wife, who is now in permanent care with Alzheimer’s disease.

Interests

I enjoy time with my dog Rambo, sitting outside in the sun, occasional visits to the pokies with a strict $20 limit, and listening to music. I used to love playing tennis and would like support to keep socially connected, including visiting my wife.

Medical History:

I have emphysema/COPD with severe breathlessness and limited exercise tolerance (about 10 metres before stopping). I have a history of depression and was admitted to a mental health ward for three weeks around six months ago following a suicide attempt. I take medications morning and night and use a puffer. My medicines are supplied in a Webster/blister pack by Chemist Warehouse. I manage my own medications and do not need prompts currently.

My mobility is limited by breathlessness and fatigue. I have been recommended a four-wheel walker but I do not use it because getting it in and out of the car and using it is exhausting. I have an Advance Care Plan (ACP) held with Geelong Hospital, and my children hold Enduring Power of Attorney; Stuart is my main point of contact.

I report occasional headaches (around 6/10) triggered by stress or tension; I sometimes take a Panadol before bed.

I experience prostate-related nocturia and get up regularly at night to toilet.

I have a history of multiple skin cancers removed and a current spot on my neck that may need removal.

I have no known allergies and I am not taking any prescribed medications.

My Care Plan

Preferred Name: Ralph

Full Name: Ralph Wakely

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

People involved in developing my care plan

I developed this plan with support from June and Stuart (main point of contact and Enduring Power of Attorney holder), and the Care Partner.

I have no specific cultural or diversity considerations for matching me with workers.

I prefer workers to communicate by speaking clearly, slowly, and a little louder due to my hearing impairment, and to check my understanding.

My family and neighbour provide informal support and social connection.

Family Background and Life History

I was born in Hamilton and moved to Portland when I was about three.

I worked for a builder, then at the Meatworks boning, and later owned a small farm, a dairy farm, and a hobby farm before moving to my current home.

I experienced a significant financial loss from an investment which affected our lives.

I enjoy walking, gardening, and going out for a coffee.

I like watching football and enjoy watching my grandkids play.

I value getting outside and doing something physical on good days.

I have a history of a hernia operation, radiation treatment in Geelong, and multiple skin cancer removals including surgery on my right ear around two to three years ago.

I have prostate-related nocturia that wakes me at night.

care_analyses.generated_html:
Care Plan

Care Alerts

I prefer care workers who speak English clearly, are respectful, easy to get along with, and do not discuss or preach religion while providing services.

I prefer a female cleaner. I am easygoing about who attends for my supports as long as they meet my preferences above.

I consent to resuscitation. In an emergency: call 000 first, then contact my daughter Elizabeth.

If there is no answer at a scheduled visit: please call me first, leave a message, and if you cannot reach me, contact Elizabeth.

I have hearing loss in my left ear. Please speak clearly and face me when talking.

I have Type 2 diabetes, a heart murmur (monitoring planned), sleep apnea, and depression (now well managed). I do not have known medication allergies documented here.

I have had bilateral knee replacements and an old right-wrist injury. I am independent with mobility, with occasional stiffness or pain (worse in cold weather).

I do not have a personal alarm or key lockbox and do not wish to install them at present.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 11 September 2025

Preferred Name: Graeme

Full Name: Graeme Bushby

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I developed this plan with my Care Partner during my assessment. My daughter Elizabeth is my preferred contact. My wife Janet’s needs were discussed in relation to scheduling, though this plan is for me, Graeme.

Care Partner (name not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided).

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I do not practice a religion and prefer that care workers keep their religious beliefs to themselves while working. Being respectful, speaking good English, being easy to get along with, and having a sense of humour are important to me.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer workers who are respectful, punctual, communicate clearly in English, and can have a friendly laugh while they work.

Please speak clearly and face me due to hearing loss in my left ear.

Cleaning is scheduled for Tuesdays at 10:00 AM for 1.5 hours. Meal preparation support is every other Tuesday at 11:30 AM for 1.5 hours. Gardening is for 2 hours every three weeks (ad hoc scheduling).

If I do not answer at a scheduled visit, please call me and leave a message. If you cannot reach me, contact Elizabeth.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination

My Preferred Support People

My wife Janet.

My daughters Elizabeth and Kate.

My friend Penny (former neighbour).

My community connections through local football clubs, the Men’s Shed, and Good Friday Appeal colleagues.

Informal Supports

My children assist me as needed. I also have supportive friends and community contacts through football clubs, the Men’s Shed, and charity events.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I grew up in Horsham with my brothers Brian (now living with dementia), Gary and John. My childhood was tough. I worked most of my life selling car parts and managing parts/service operations, including at Jetty Toyota for 10–15 years. I retired about five years ago after knee replacements.

Interests

I am active in local football clubs (3–4 days a week), attend the Men’s Shed twice weekly, and help with community and charity events such as the Good Friday Appeal, MS Australia bike rides, and the Great Vic Bike Ride. I enjoy staying active, helping others, and being part of my community.

My Medical Information

Medical History

Type 2 diabetes.

Heart murmur; periodic cardiac monitoring is planned in about two months.

Sleep apnea.

Depression (previously significant low mood; now improved with supports and staying active).

Bilateral total knee replacements (functioning well). Old right wrist injury with reduced function and stiffness.

No falls history reported.

Medication

I take my prescribed medications daily. My medicines are supplied in a blister pack through my pharmacy. I self-manage and do not need assistance. No allergies were reported in this transcript.

Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Mobility and Equipment

I mobilise independently without walking aids and continue to drive. I can get in and out of the car independently.

I have a recliner/lift chair. I do not use a shower chair or handrails (these are in the home for Janet).

GP / Pharmacy

GP: Dr Morrison, Monash Health Centre (address not documented in this transcript).

Pharmacy: Cranburn Community Pharmacy, 32–36 Remont Way.

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

CALD: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Living with disability (mobility): I have had both knees replaced and an old right wrist injury; I mobilise independently but can be stiff or sore with cold weather.

Mental health (low mood/isolation risk): I have a history of depression and reported past thoughts of suicidality earlier in the year; I am currently stable and supported by family, friends, and community activities.

Specific Risks

  • No key lockbox and no personal alarm by choice, which could delay emergency access.
  • Hearing impairment (left ear) may affect communication if not addressed.
  • Diabetes self-management requires ongoing adherence to medication and diet.
  • Intermittent knee and wrist pain (worse in cold weather) may affect function on some days.
  • No formal written Advance Care Directive or Enduring Power of Attorney in place; daughter Elizabeth is nominated verbally.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

Primary contact: Elizabeth (daughter). Phone not documented in this transcript.

Other important people: Janet (wife), Kate (daughter).

Emergency instructions while workers are present: Call 000 first, commence resuscitation if required, then contact Elizabeth.

If no response at a scheduled visit: Call me and leave a message. If I cannot be reached, contact Elizabeth.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will keep my home clean and safe so I am not straining my knees or wrist, and so I can stay active with my football clubs and Men’s Shed.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I am independent but experience knee and wrist pain in cold weather. A consistent weekly clean reduces physical strain and trip hazards.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo HomeCare will provide Domestic Assistance to vacuum, mop, clean bathrooms, dust benches, and manage linens weekly on Tuesdays at 10:00 AM (1.5 hours).

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare support worker and me to guide priorities. When will it be done?: Weekly, over the next 3 months (quarter), Tuesdays 10:00–11:30 AM. How much will it cost?: $85/hour x 1.5 hours x 4 weeks = $510/month (approx. $1,530 per quarter).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 2 Goal: I will maintain my yard and outdoor access so pathways are safe and tidy, supporting my independence and community activities.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can manage most tasks but outdoor work can aggravate my knees and wrist.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo HomeCare will provide Light Home & Gardening Maintenance for mowing, weeding, and light pruning for 2 hours every three weeks (ad hoc scheduling).

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare gardener and me to specify tasks. When will it be done?: Every three weeks over the next 3 months. How much will it cost?: $85/hour x 2 hours every 3 weeks ≈ $227/month (approx. $680 per quarter).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 3 Goal: I will have help with meal preparation every fortnight so that meals are ready and safe to manage at home, especially when my wrist is sore and to support Janet when needed.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I eat well and take my medications; occasional wrist and knee pain can make meal tasks harder.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo HomeCare will provide assistance with meal preparation and kitchen clean-up for 1.5 hours every other Tuesday at 11:30 AM, including optional supported shopping if required.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare support worker and me to choose menus and tasks. When will it be done?: Fortnightly over the next 3 months. How much will it cost?: $85/hour x 1.5 hours x 2 visits/month = $255/month (approx. $765 per quarter).

Care Plan

Care Alerts

I am hard of hearing and I need care workers to speak slowly, clearly and loudly in English so I can understand.

I have a falls risk due to reduced balance and I must use my four-wheel walker at all times when mobilising.

I am currently taking blood thinners and I bruise easily, so I have an increased risk of bleeding if I fall or sustain a cut.

I have a chronic head wound that has been stable for months and I self-manage a dry dressing nightly.

I experience arthritis pain in my fingers, elbows and knees, a right-leg spasm, and burning feet at night which can disturb my sleep and mobility.

I have a wheeze that has been worse since COVID, and I am an ex-smoker who quit about 50 years ago.

I am virtually blind in my left eye which increases my falls risk, especially in low light.

I have slight urinary incontinence and use level 2 continence pads (Tenar brand) at approximately $40 per month.

I am allergic to house dust mites and regular dusting and linen changes help reduce symptoms.

I have a personal alarm through my retirement village that I can press to call for help, and it is not a falls detector.

I prefer workers to knock and enter to check on me if I do not answer for a scheduled visit, as the door is usually unlocked during the day.

I have a key lockbox for emergencies only (code 8933) and workers must use it only if there is no other way to safely enter.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 15 September 2025

Preferred Name: Peter

Full Name: Peter Cram

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I participated in this assessment and I make my own decisions.

My family member attended the assessment and supports me, and I have an Enduring Power of Attorney held by a family member.

The care partner/assessor facilitated this care planning discussion, and my ongoing Care Partner will be Cassie (as introduced by the provider).

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I was born in Metara, Australia, and I do not currently practice a religion.

My core values are family, independence, honesty and integrity, and I want my care to respect these values.

I do not have specific cultural customs or diversity needs I want recognised beyond my communication needs related to hearing.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer workers who speak clear English and will talk slowly, clearly and loudly because I am hard of hearing.

I want workers to knock first and use the door to enter for scheduled visits, and to use the lockbox only in an emergency.

I want regular and reliable scheduling: Domestic Assistance on Tuesdays 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM and Social Support on Thursdays 11:00 AM to 1:30 PM.

I prefer companionship-based Social Support that includes playing Scrabble and conversation, and I do not want to go shopping as I shop online.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination.

My Preferred Support People

My family, including my two sons and grandchildren, are important to me and are my preferred support people.

Staff at my retirement village are supportive and available if needed.

Informal Supports

I live in a retirement village where staff can assist in emergencies and there is a site fire plan.

I keep in touch with family, including Zoom calls with my son twice a week.

I attend a book club and monthly social dinners at my residence.

I will continue with my physiotherapy through Polina Healthcare, and I see a podiatrist for foot care.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I grew up in a small country town and went to boarding school from age 10 for three years, which I enjoyed.

I was a pharmacist and owned pharmacies in Castelan and Geelong, and I also worked as a relieving pharmacist.

My late wife was also a pharmacist, we met at pharmacy college, and we were married for 64 years, knowing each other for nearly 70 years.

I have two sons and family is very important to me.

I played football until age 27 and used to enjoy bowls and going to the gym regularly.

Interests

I enjoy reading books and the newspaper, watching television including football, cricket and documentaries, and I have an interest in politics.

I attend a book club and monthly social dinners at my retirement village.

Loneliness is my biggest problem and I value companionship, including having someone to play Scrabble with me.

My Medical Information

Medical History

I have a history of a broken leg around three years ago and I am cautious about falls.

I have had cancer treatments about three years ago.

I have high blood pressure that is under control and a heart flutter.

I have GORD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) that is under control.

I have hearing loss and wear hearing aids.

I have a chronic head wound that has been stable for months and I self-manage a nightly dry dressing.

I experience arthritis in my fingers, elbows and knees, and a right-leg spasm that is being monitored.

I experience burning feet syndrome that is worse at night.

I have a wheeze that has been worse since I had COVID; I am an ex-smoker who quit about 50 years ago.

I have slight urinary incontinence and require one pad per day.

I am virtually blind in my left eye.

I notice some forgetfulness but I have not been assessed for dementia.

Medication

I self-manage my medications and do not need assistance.

I take Pelixia twice daily and paracetamol for arthritis pain.

I have been on blood thinners for a couple of months.

I use liniment on my knees and elbows when needed.

I have an allergy to house dust mites and no known medication allergies.

Mobility and Equipment

I cannot walk without my four-wheel walker and I sometimes use walking sticks for short trips.

I have a shower chair, handrails in the shower, a recliner chair, a bed transfer pole and a personal alarm.

I do not have a raised toilet seat and I do not use any mechanical lifters.

GP / Pharmacy

GP: Dr. Mabo, Manningham General Practice (200 High Street).

Pharmacy: Terry White Pharmacy, 45 Were Street, Montmorency.

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

CALD: No, I am Australian-born and speak English.

Living with disability (mobility): Yes, I have reduced balance and require a four-wheel walker.

Mental health (low mood/isolation risk): Yes, I report loneliness and I value companionship.

Specific Risks

I am at risk of falls due to impaired balance, vision changes and fatigue.

I am at increased bleeding risk due to blood thinners and easy bruising.

I have a chronic head wound that can ooze at night and may become infected if not monitored.

I have hearing impairment which can affect communication and safety if instructions are missed.

I have a wheeze post-COVID which may affect my breathing and exercise tolerance.

I have burning feet at night which may disturb sleep and contribute to unsteadiness.

I have slight urinary incontinence which may increase skin irritation risk and slipping risk if pads are not managed.

I prefer my door to be unlocked during the day and I allow entry if I do not answer, which requires clear worker identification and safety protocols.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

In a medical emergency, I want workers to call Triple Zero (000), commence first aid/CPR as trained, and notify my family/EPOA.

My personal alarm connects me to the monitoring service when I press the button and they will stay on the phone until help arrives.

If I do not answer for a scheduled visit, I want workers to enter and check on me, as my door is usually unlocked during the day.

The key lockbox code is 8933 and it is for emergency use only.

There is a site fire plan in my retirement village and staff can assist during facility emergencies.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will feel less lonely by having a Salveo HomeCare support worker visit to play Scrabble and provide companionship every Thursday 11:00 AM–1:30 PM so I can enjoy conversation and mental stimulation.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I am independent with personal care but I am hard of hearing, I fatigue easily, and I have a falls risk; I prefer to stay in rather than go shopping.

How will we do this? (Tasks): The worker will arrive on time, speak slowly and clearly, play Scrabble and other brain teasers with me, and check in on my wellbeing. If I choose to go for a short walk or coffee, the worker will support me with my four-wheel walker and transport if planned.

Service Category: Independence Support

GOAL 2 Goal: I will maintain a clean, low-dust and safe home so I can live independently and comfortably, with focus on dusting and linen changes to reduce my house-dust mite allergy.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I cannot safely do heavier cleaning due to reduced balance, fatigue and arthritis; I am at increased bleeding risk on blood thinners.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo HomeCare will provide Domestic Assistance on Tuesdays 11:00 AM–1:00 PM for vacuuming, mopping, bathroom/toilet clean, kitchen surfaces, dusting shelves and high-touch areas, and changing bed linen weekly to reduce dust mites.

Who is responsible?: I am, with Salveo HomeCare Domestic Assistance. When will it be done?: Weekly for 2 hours on Tuesdays, over the next 3 months. How much will it cost?: Domestic Assistance $85/hour x 2 hours weekly ≈ $680/month.

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 3 Goal: I will keep my mobility and balance by continuing weekly physiotherapy and my home exercise program so I can walk safely with my four-wheel walker for 10–15 minutes most days and reduce right-leg spasms.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I require my four-wheel walker for all walking, I have a falls risk, a left-eye vision deficit, and I fatigue during the day.

(Tasks): I will receive Allied Health therapy (physiotherapy) weekly for 1 hour to progress balance and gait, and I will complete my physio home exercises for 10–15 minutes at least 5 days per week. care_analyses.generated_html:
Care Plan

Care Alerts

  • Allergy: I am allergic to theatre tape/adhesive tape (significant skin reaction after prior surgery).

  • Mental health: I live with OCD with a strong phobia of dust (fear, not an allergy), and I experience anxiety.

  • Falls risk: I have had approximately 10–12 falls in the past year, often related to rushing to the bathroom due to urinary urgency. I use a walker and have balance difficulties, especially when turning quickly.

  • Wound care: I require lower limb wound dressings three times per week.

  • Pain: I have constant foot pain that disturbs sleep and impacts mobility.

  • Medication sensitivity: I ceased Lyrica due to sedation and increased falls.

  • Mobility: I rely on a walker, furniture-walk indoors at times, and must enter cars from the left side due to right knee replacement limitations.

  • Emergency response preference: If I am found unconscious or not breathing, call 000 first, commence resuscitation/CPR, then call my family.

  • End-of-life spiritual preference: When the time comes, I would like access to a priest or pastoral care.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 16 September 2025

Preferred Name: Denise

Full Name: Denise Ruxton

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I participated in this assessment and care planning discussion to describe my needs and preferences.

My husband, Bruce, contributed information about our daily routines and preferences.

An assessing care partner/care coordinator facilitated the assessment and care planning.

My son, Lee, holds my Enduring Power of Attorney and has my advance care plan documents; he will be consulted as needed.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I identify as Catholic. God and family are most important to me, and honesty matters. I would like to be more assertive.

I am heterosexual. I do not have any specific cultural constraints for worker matching and I am comfortable with male or female workers.

Because I have OCD with a phobia of dust, I feel safer and calmer when my environment is kept clean and low-dust.

When end-of-life approaches, I would value the opportunity to speak with a priest or pastoral care from any church.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer workers to be aware of my OCD and dust phobia so they can explain what they are doing and keep areas dust-free where possible.

Clear, calm communication helps me when I feel anxious. On busy days, coordinating visits together (e.g., nurse with Bruce’s personal care) helps reduce disruption and stress.

For emergencies during scheduled visits, please call 000 first, commence CPR if indicated, then contact my family. If there is no answer at my door, call my mobile, check with neighbours/management, and there is a key held in the office for access by authorised personnel.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination.

My Preferred Support People

My husband Bruce is my closest support person.

My children Amanda and Lee, and Lee’s wife Tracey, are important to me. My grandchildren and great-grandchildren are also important in my life.

Informal Supports

Bruce and I support each other day-to-day at home.

Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the second of four sisters in a Catholic family. I trained as a nurse at St Vincent’s Hospital in Melbourne and worked across surgical and palliative care settings over many years. Mid-career, I experienced burnout and trained in social work, working with homeless men in North Melbourne, before returning to nursing at a repatriation hospital in Tasmania, including night palliative care shifts. I married Bruce in 1962; we recently celebrated our 63rd anniversary. We have children and a growing family of grandchildren and great-grandchildren. I retired around age 59 and found the transition away from work challenging at first.

Interests

Bruce makes me happy—especially when he is smiling. Family time matters. I enjoy reading magazines (e.g., Country Life), but I often feel I don’t have time. I would like to get breakfast earlier in the day and then get on with the household tasks I want to complete. I am considering going out to a café with Bruce for breakfast every second morning after our move.

My Medical Information

Medical History: I have OCD with a specific phobia of dust and I experience anxiety. I had a mental health breakdown in 1984. I have a right knee replacement; a right mastectomy for breast cancer with several prior lumpectomies; a minor stroke in 2010 with residual numbness on the left side (especially fingers); broken bones in my hand after a fall; a prior broken toe; and a foot injury about a year ago when a taxi ran over my foot requiring a moon boot for seven weeks. I report bunions (right worse) and hammertoes (right worse). I experience shortness of breath when walking up inclines. I report a possible facial skin lesion that needs a skin specialist review. I have ongoing lower limb wounds requiring dressings three times per week.

Medication: I use a blister pack for my prescribed medications. I am taking medication to assist with urinary urgency (name not stated). For pain, I take Panadol—two tablets when pain spikes, up to every four hours (not every day). I previously trialled Lyrica for neuropathic pain but stopped due to sleepiness and increased falls. I do not require assistance with medications, injections, or patches.

Mobility and Equipment: I require a walker to mobilise and sometimes furniture-walk indoors. My main difficulty is balance, especially when turning too quickly. I enter cars from the left side due to right knee limitations. I sleep in a chair at times; I want OT support to help me return to bed safely. I have an over-toilet aid and use continence pads as needed.

GP / Pharmacy: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

CALD: I speak English and identify as Catholic; no interpreter required.

Living with disability (mobility): I have significant falls risk, balance problems, and rely on a walker.

Mental health (low mood/isolation risk): I experience anxiety, OCD, and can feel overwhelmed by household tasks; I often stay inside, which may limit social connection.

Specific Risks

  • High falls risk associated with balance impairment and rushing to the toilet due to urinary urgency.

  • Skin integrity risk due to lower limb wounds and foot deformities (bunions/hammertoes); risk of infection if dressings become wet between nurse visits.

  • Medication-related risk: prior sedation with Lyrica increased falls; now ceased.

  • Pain-related sleep disruption leading to fatigue and increased fall risk.

  • Environmental/psychological triggers: OCD with dust phobia; cluttered benches increase anxiety.

  • Transfer risk getting into vehicles (requires left-side entry and time to position leg).

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

Emergency Instructions: If I am found unconscious or not breathing during a scheduled visit, call 000 first, commence resuscitation/CPR, then call my family. If there is no answer at my door at a scheduled visit, call my mobile, check with neighbours/management, and note there is a key held in the office for authorised access.

Contacts: Bruce (husband); Amanda (daughter); Lee (son, Enduring Power of Attorney); Tracey (daughter-in-law). Phone numbers not documented in this transcript.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will keep my leg/foot wounds clean, dry and healing so I can sleep better and move with less pain over the next 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can report when dressings feel wet or uncomfortable. I have a high falls risk and foot deformities that make dressing placement tricky. Wet dressings increase infection risk.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo Registered Nurse will complete wound assessments and dressings on Monday, Wednesday and Friday; I will notify the nurse if dressings become wet; I will avoid rushing to the bathroom and use continence pads as needed between visits.

Who is responsible?: Salveo Registered Nurse and me. When will it be done?: 3 times per week (Mon/Wed/Fri), 1 hour each, mornings around 9–10 am as scheduled, for 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: $148.50/hour x 3 hours/week x 4.33 weeks/month ≈ $1,929/month.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 2 Goal: I will improve my balance and confidence walking indoors with my walker so I have fewer falls (target: zero falls requiring medical review) over the next 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I use a walker, understand I need to slow down and not turn quickly, and I have had 10–12 falls in the past year.

How will we do this? (Tasks): I will receive Allied Health Physiotherapy to review gait, balance, and set a daily home exercise plan; I will practice my indoor walking program daily at a safe pace and use the walker at all times.

Who is responsible?: Allied Health Physiotherapist and me. When will it be done?: 1 hour monthly review + daily home exercises for 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: $180/hour x 1 = $180/month.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 3 Goal: I will reduce foot pain and protect skin around bunions and hammertoes so dressings stay intact between nurse visits and I can tolerate footwear better over the next 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I have right-sided bunion and hammertoes (right worse) and fragile skin between toes from past friction and falls.

How will we do this? (Tasks): I will receive Podiatry for nail and skin care, pressure relief advice, and footwear/toe protection recommendations; I will follow podiatry advice and alert the nurse if new rubbing or skin breaks occur.

Who is responsible?: Allied Health Podiatrist and me. When will it be done?: 1 hour every 6–8 weeks (home visit). How much will it cost?: $180/hour ≈ 0.62 sessions/month ≈ $111/month (averaged).

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 4 Goal: I will safely transition from sleeping in a chair back to sleeping in my bed with the right equipment and techniques within 12 weeks to improve sleep and reduce pain.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can follow instructions but need strategies for bed entry/exit due to my knee replacement and balance issues.

How will we do this? (Tasks): I will have an Occupational Therapy assessment to set up bed, seating and transfer techniques and advise on any equipment; I will practice the recommended techniques daily.

Who is responsible?: Occupational Therapist and me. When will it be done?: Initial assessment in the first month; follow-up as recommended. How much will it cost?: $180/hour (estimate 1 hour in month one; additional sessions if recommended).

Service Category: Clinical Care

Budget and Service Classifications

Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded) / Independence Support / Everyday Living

  • Clinical Care: Registered Nurse wound care (Mon/Wed/Fri, 1 hr each); Allied Health Physiotherapy (1 hr monthly); Allied Health Podiatry (1 hr every 6–8 weeks); Occupational Therapy assessment (initial, then as recommended).

  • Everyday Living: Domestic assistance for cleaning/stocking washing/kitchen benches (weekly, day noted as Thursday; duration to be scheduled); Meal delivery service (client-selected provider); Transport via taxi card budget.

  • Independence Support: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Quarterly Budget Allocation

Estimated monthly Clinical Care costs based on agreed services:

  • Registered Nurse wound care: ≈ $1,929/month.

  • Physiotherapy: $180/month.

  • Podiatry: ≈ $111/month (average across 6–8 week cycle).

  • Occupational Therapy: $180 in the first month (estimate), then as recommended.

Estimated Clinical Care subtotal per month (excluding OT follow-ups): ≈ $2,220/month. Estimated Clinical Care subtotal per quarter (3 months): ≈ $6,660. One-off OT assessment adds ≈ $180 in the first quarter.

Everyday Living costs (domestic assistance, meals, transport) are to be scheduled/ordered and will be costed once service durations and suppliers are confirmed.

Summary 
The meeting transcript documents a care assessment interview between a healthcare worker and Denise, an elderly woman. The healthcare worker is collecting comprehensive information to create a care profile for Denise and her husband Bruce, who are moving to a new home in Ballarat. 
The assessment begins with questions about Denise's cultural background, where she reveals she has OCD with a particular phobia of dust. She mentions having experienced a mental breakdown in 1984 and discusses her core values, identifying God and family as most important to her, along with honesty. She expresses a desire to be more assertive. 
Denise provides her Medicare information and confirms she is responsible for making her own decisions, though sometimes she's not quick with them. When discussing end-of-life preferences, she mentions wanting to speak with a priest or pastoral care when the time comes. 
The healthcare worker collects emergency contact information and establishes protocols for scheduled visits, including what to do if Denise is found unconscious (call triple zero, perform resuscitation, and call family). Denise shares that care workers need to know about her OCD and dust phobia, and mentions she has an allergy to theater tape. 
When discussing her daily routine, Denise explains that a good day involves having breakfast early and getting to work on household tasks she wants to accomplish. She identifies anxiety as a significant issue, describing herself as "a worrier." Bad days involve getting up grumpy and experiencing heightened anxiety and OCD symptoms. She acknowledges needing to relax more and appreciates help with household tasks like washing stockings and kitchen cleaning. 
Denise shares her life history, including being the second of four sisters, training as a nurse at St. Vincent's Hospital in Melbourne, getting married at 22, and having children shortly after. She worked as a nurse for many years, took a break due to burnout, pursued social work training, and then returned to nursing, working in palliative care before retiring around age 59. 
The healthcare worker assesses Denise's current health status, noting she experiences constant pain, particularly in her feet, which affects her mobility and sleep. She uses a walker and has had 10-12 falls in the past year. She has had several medical procedures including a right knee replacement, right mastectomy, and broken bones in her hand and foot. She requires wound dressings three times a week and has issues with her feet including bunions and hammertoes. 
The assessment concludes with arrangements for various services including nursing visits for wound care (Monday, Wednesday, Friday), domestic assistance (Thursdays), physiotherapy, occupational therapy assessment, podiatry, meal delivery, and taxi services. The healthcare worker emphasizes that this comprehensive assessment will help build a profile to ensure care workers understand how Denise and Bruce like things done. 
Chapters 
Cultural Background and Core Values Assessment ‎ 00:00:00
The healthcare worker begins the assessment by asking Denise about her cultural background and any traditions, languages, or customs that might impact her care. Denise reveals she has OCD with a particular phobia of dust (D-U-S-T) and mentions having had a "mental breakdown" in 1984. When asked about her core values, Denise identifies God as her "best friend really, apart from Bruce," followed by family and honesty. She expresses a desire to be more assertive. Denise confirms that God is very important to her but states there are no specific cultural factors to consider when matching her with a care worker. 
Personal Information and Decision-Making ‎ 00:03:08
The healthcare worker collects Denise's Medicare information (2274499253, position 2) and asks about her decision-making capacity. Denise confirms she is responsible for making her own decisions but acknowledges she's "not quick with decisions" sometimes. When discussing end-of-life preferences, Denise mentions she would want to talk to a priest or any pastoral church representative. She references that her son Lee has an enduring power of attorney and advanced care plan in place. 
Emergency Protocols and Special Considerations ‎ 00:06:36
The healthcare worker establishes protocols for scheduled visits and emergency situations. If care workers arrive and Denise is unconscious or not breathing, they will call triple zero, perform resuscitation, and then call family. Denise identifies important information for care workers, including her OCD, dust phobia (fear, not allergy), and an allergy to theater tape that caused issues after a past surgery. The healthcare worker notes these special considerations for Denise's care profile. 
Daily Routine and Quality of Life Assessment ‎ 00:10:27
Denise describes what keeps her healthy and safe, including taking medications on time, eating well, and trying to drink enough fluids. She acknowledges needing to do more exercises at home but struggles with time management. A good day for Denise involves having breakfast early enough and getting to work on household tasks she wants to accomplish. A bad day involves getting up grumpy, experiencing communication difficulties with Bruce, and heightened anxiety. Denise identifies her anxiety as a significant issue, describing herself as "a worrier" who worries about "two flies crawling up the wall." She acknowledges needing to relax more and appreciates help with household tasks like washing stockings and kitchen cleaning. 
Social Connections and Life Satisfaction ‎ 00:19:44
When asked what makes her happy, Denise immediately identifies Bruce, particularly "Bruce smiling, not frowning." She also mentions family, including grandchildren, as important sources of happiness, though she notes they don't call very often. Denise lists important people in her life: Bruce first, followed by her children Amanda and Lee, Lee's wife Tracey, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, plus "the odd friend." She expresses concern about visitors seeing a messy kitchen when they come to her home and mentions feeling like she doesn't have time for social activities at the retirement village. 
Life History and Career ‎ 00:21:59
Denise shares her life history as the second of four sisters in a Catholic family. She trained as a nurse at St. Vincent's Hospital in Melbourne after briefly working in a secretarial job. She married Bruce at age 22 in 1962 (celebrating their 63rd anniversary recently) and had their first child, Amanda, about 11 months after marriage. Denise took a break from nursing while her children were young but returned to work later. Midway through her career, she experienced burnout and left nursing temporarily to pursue social work training. She worked with homeless men in North Melbourne before eventually returning to nursing at a repatriation hospital in Tasmania, where she did palliative care, often working nights. She retired around age 59 and initially felt a loss when she stopped receiving calls to come in for shifts. 
Current Health Status and Medical History ‎ 00:37:40
The healthcare worker assesses Denise's current health status. Denise reports experiencing anger due to stress and pain, particularly in her feet. Her medical history includes a right knee replacement, right mastectomy for "fairly large cancer" with several prior lumpectomies, broken bones in her hand, a minor stroke in 2010 affecting her left side with residual numbness, and a foot injury when a taxi ran over it, requiring her to wear a "moon boot" for seven weeks. Denise reports constant pain, particularly in her feet, which affects her mobility and sleep. She takes Panadol (two tablets every four hours) when pain spikes but had to stop taking Lyrica due to side effects of sleepiness and falls. 
Mobility Assessment and Fall History ‎ 00:46:01
Denise requires a walker for mobility and identifies balance as her main difficulty, along with turning too quickly and not walking slowly enough. She reports having had 10-12 falls in the past year, with the worst being two falls in one week after New Year's. She mentions that falls often occur when she's rushing to the bathroom due to urinary urgency. Denise describes difficulty getting into cars, needing to approach from the left side due to limited flexibility in her right leg following knee replacement surgery. She has foot problems including bunions (particularly on the right foot) and hammertoes, which complicate her wound dressings.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 16 September 2025

Preferred Name: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Full Name: Denise Ruxton

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Interpreter required?: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

I participated in this assessment and planning conversation with a care partner (assessor).

My husband Bruce contributed context about our daily routines.

My son Lee holds enduring power of attorney and has my advance care plan; he is a key support person for decisions.

I am Catholic and said that God is very important to me; I value God, family, and honesty. I would like to be more assertive.

I am comfortable with either male or female workers.

I identify as heterosexual.

At end of life I would like to speak with a priest or pastoral care (or a counsellor/social worker if preferred at the time).

My OCD (particularly a phobia of dust) affects how I feel in my home. Keeping visible surfaces clear helps reduce my anxiety.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer workers to be on time, explain what they are going to do, check in about my anxiety/OCD on the day, and avoid creating dust. Calm, clear communication helps me.

I am comfortable with male or female workers.

When possible, I prefer to coordinate visits together (e.g., my nurse visit while Bruce’s personal care occurs) so our day is not broken up. Monday mornings around 9–10am have worked previously.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination

My Preferred Support People

Bruce (husband).

Amanda (daughter) and Lee (son). Lee’s wife Tracey.

Grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

For pastoral care, I would like access to a priest or church representative when needed.

Informal Supports

I live with my husband Bruce. My family (Amanda and Lee, and extended family) are important to me and can be contacted if needed. Lee is my enduring power of attorney.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the second of four sisters and was raised Catholic. I trained and worked as a nurse (including palliative care and night duty), took time out for social work training and worked with homeless men, then returned to nursing. I retired around age 59. Bruce and I married in 1962 and recently celebrated our 63rd anniversary. We are moving to a new home in Ballarat. We have children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

Interests

I enjoy time with Bruce and family. I like home tasks and keeping things in order, but my anxiety and OCD can make me feel I must stay inside to “keep up.” I would like to relax more and have breakfast earlier in the morning. I worry about visitors seeing a messy kitchen.

My Medical Information

Medical History:

Right knee replacement (limited ability to get the right leg far back; I enter cars from the left side).

Right mastectomy for a large cancer; multiple prior lumpectomies.

Minor stroke in 2010 with residual numbness on the left side (fingers more affected).

Multiple falls; three broken bones in my hand after a fall (around last Christmas).

Foot run over by a taxi about a year ago; wore a moon boot for seven weeks.

Foot problems: bunion on right foot and hammertoes (right worse than left).

Possible skin cancer on my face — plan to see a skin specialist.

History of nausea after anaesthetic in the distant past (noted during recovery years ago).

OCD with prominent phobia of dust; anxiety.

Medication:

I use blister packs and manage my own medications.

Pain: Panadol — I take two tablets when pain spikes (up to every four hours, not every day).

Previously on Lyrica for nerve pain, stopped due to sleepiness and increased falls.

Bladder urgency medication (name not recalled) prescribed by my GP.

I use a walker and sometimes “furniture walk.” My main difficulty is balance, turning too quickly, and rushing (especially to the bathroom due to urgency). I get short of breath on inclines.

I have an over-toilet aid. I wear compression stockings that need washing weekly.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can direct tasks and explain my preferences; anxiety and dust phobia increase when surfaces are cluttered.

Who is responsible?: I am, with Salveo Domestic Assistance; When will it be done?: 1 hour weekly for 3 months; How much will it cost?: $85/hour, approximately $368/month.

Service Category: Clinical Care

Who is responsible?: I am, with Salveo Social Support worker; When will it be done?: 1 hour fortnightly for 3 months; How much will it cost?: $85/hour, approximately $184/month (no transport required).

Budget and Service Classifications

Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded) / Independence Support / Everyday Living

Quarterly Budget Allocation: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Classification Level (1-8 under Support at Home): Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

I agree with this care plan and the goals we have set together. I consent to Salveo HomeCare coordinating and delivering the services listed, and to sharing this plan with my chosen support people and relevant health professionals (e.g., my GP, nursing/allied health) for safe, coordinated care.

risks.description: High fall frequency (approx. 10–12 in the past year), balance issues, turns too quickly, rushes to toilet due to urinary urgency; has struck head and required CT; uses walker.
Ongoing foot wounds requiring dressings three times weekly; bunions and hammertoes complicate dressings; risk of moisture-related breakdown.
High anxiety and OCD with pronounced dust phobia; stress can lead to anger and worsened symptoms.
Constant foot pain affecting sleep and mobility; requires PRN analgesia; prior neuropathic agent ceased due to adverse effects.
Urinary urgency leads to rushing to the bathroom and contributes to falls; uses continence pads; on bladder medication.
Allergic reaction to theatre/adhesive tape.
Difficulty getting into cars; must enter from the left due to right knee replacement and limited flexibility.
Mild shortness of breath on inclines.
Tends to stay inside and limit social activities; feels tied to household routines and worries about home presentation to visitors.

care_analyses.generated_html:
Care Plan

Care Alerts

  • I have a high falls risk (about 10–12 falls in the past year), mainly due to balance issues and rushing to the bathroom because of urinary urgency. I use a walker and sometimes “furniture walk.”

  • I need wound dressings three times a week. Dressings can become wet, particularly on the left foot, and need checking between nurse visits.

  • I experience constant foot pain that affects my sleep and mobility. I take two Panadol when pain spikes and I no longer take Lyrica due to sleepiness and falls.

  • I have OCD with a specific phobia of dust. Anxiety is often high and can be triggered by mess, especially visible kitchen clutter.

  • I am allergic/sensitive to theatre tape (adhesive). Please avoid theatre tape and strong adhesive products; use hypoallergenic alternatives.

  • If I am found unconscious or not breathing, please call 000 immediately, commence resuscitation (CPR), and then call my family.

  • Access and welfare checks: If I do not answer for a scheduled visit, call my mobile, check with neighbours and village management, and note there is a key held in the office.

  • I have reduced flexibility in my right knee (post replacement) and need to enter vehicles from the left side for safer transfers.

  • I often sleep in a chair; I want Occupational Therapy support to return to sleeping safely in my bed.

  • My Catholic faith is important to me. At end of life, I would like to speak with a priest or pastoral care.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 16 September 2025

Preferred Name: Denise

Full Name: Denise Ruxton

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Interpreter required?: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

People involved in developing my care plan

I developed this plan with the Care Partner during my assessment. My husband Bruce contributed during the discussion. My son Lee holds my Enduring Power of Attorney and has my advance care plan.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I identify as Catholic and my faith in God and my family are most important to me. Honesty is a core value for me and I would like to be more assertive.

I am heterosexual. I do not have a preference for the gender of workers.

At end of life, I would like to speak with a priest or pastoral church representative.

My OCD includes a specific phobia of dust; keeping visible spaces (especially the kitchen) orderly helps me feel calm.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I am comfortable with male or female workers.

Please be aware of my OCD and dust phobia when planning tasks. Keeping bench tops tidy on entry reduces my anxiety.

I prefer morning bookings when possible so I can use the rest of the day for my own activities. A 9:00–10:00am window has worked well for combined visits with Bruce’s supports.

For missed visit checks, please call my mobile, check with neighbours/management, and note there is a key kept in the office.

For vehicle transfers, please position the car so I can enter from the left due to my right knee’s reduced bend.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination.

My Preferred Support People

My husband Bruce is my primary support. My children Amanda and Lee, and Lee’s wife Tracey, are important to me. My grandchildren and great-grandchildren are also important in my life.

Informal Supports

Bruce supports me day to day. I manage my own medications using blister packs. Family are available as needed.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the second of four sisters and I was raised Catholic. I trained and worked as a nurse (St Vincent’s Hospital, Melbourne), took time off while my children were young, later trained in social work and worked with homeless men in North Melbourne, then returned to nursing in palliative care (including night duty) before retiring around age 59. Bruce and I married in 1962 and recently celebrated our 63rd anniversary. We are moving to a new home in Ballarat.

Interests

I enjoy time with Bruce and family. I like to keep my home organised and clean. I would like to relax more and allow myself time to enjoy reading, but I often feel I don’t have time due to routines and my OCD.

My Medical Information

Medical History: I have OCD (dust phobia) and experienced a mental breakdown in 1984. I had a right knee replacement; a right mastectomy for breast cancer following several lumpectomies; a minor stroke in 2010 affecting my left side with residual numbness (especially in the fingers); multiple falls; three hand bones fractured after a fall (late last year); a prior foot injury when a taxi ran over my foot (wore a moon boot for seven weeks); a history of a broken toe; bunions (right worse) and hammertoes (right worse). I report possible skin cancer on my face that I will seek review for. I experience urinary urgency. I experience shortness of breath on inclines. I have constant foot pain that disturbs my sleep.

Medication: I manage my medications independently using blister packs. I take Panadol (two tablets when pain spikes, up to every four hours, not every day). I previously tried Lyrica for neuropathic pain but stopped due to sleepiness and increased falls. I take a bladder/urgency medication (name not recorded). I do not require assistance with injections, patches, or blood sugar monitoring.

Mobility and Equipment: I require a walker to mobilise and sometimes “furniture walk.” My balance is my main difficulty, especially when turning or rushing. I have an over-toilet aid. I prefer car entry from the left side due to limited right knee flexion. I currently sleep in a chair but want to return to safe bed sleeping with OT support. I use/wash support stockings with assistance weekly.

GP / Pharmacy: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

I do not identify specific CALD needs. I am living with mobility limitations and a high falls risk. I live with anxiety and OCD, and I can feel isolated when I keep to my routines and avoid social activities.

Specific Risks

  • Falls risk due to balance issues and rushing to the bathroom with urinary urgency.

  • Wound complications if dressings become wet or are not changed as scheduled.

  • Anxiety/OCD triggers related to dust and visible clutter (especially kitchen areas).

  • Pain-related sleep disturbance and daytime fatigue affecting safety and mood.

  • Allergy to theatre tape/strong adhesives causing skin reactions.

  • Car transfers are higher risk; I require left-side entry and extra time.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

If I am found unconscious or not breathing during a scheduled visit: call 000 immediately, commence resuscitation (CPR), and then call my family.

If I do not answer the door for a scheduled visit: call my mobile, check with neighbours and management, and access the key held in the office if required.

My Enduring Power of Attorney is my son, Lee. My daughter is Amanda. Contact numbers are not documented in this transcript.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will have my lower limb/foot wounds professionally managed so they remain clean, dry and healing, with fewer wet dressings and no infections over the next 3 months.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can monitor my dressings and alert the nurse if they become wet (left foot wetness happens most). I have a high falls risk and constant foot pain which can slow healing.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo Registered Nurse will complete wound assessments and dressings on Monday, Wednesday and Friday; educate me on checking for wet dressings and red flags; coordinate supplies; document wound measurements fortnightly to track healing.

Who is responsible?: Salveo Registered Nurse and me. When will it be done?: 3 times weekly for the next 3 months (quarter). How much will it cost?: $148.50/hour x 1 hour x 3 times weekly ≈ 12 hours/month = $1,782/month (Clinical Care is 100% government funded).
