Abilities and considerations (risks): I use a walker and understand I rush and turn too quickly. Urinary urgency can make me hurry and increases falls risk.

GOAL 3 Goal: I will return to sleeping safely in my bed (instead of the chair) at least 5 nights per week within 3 months so my overnight pain and wake-ups reduce.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I currently sleep in a chair due to pain and difficulty with bed transfers. I wake overnight due to pain and bladder urgency.

(Tasks): Salveo Allied Health Occupational Therapist will complete a home OT assessment to recommend bed mobility strategies and equipment; I will trial the recommendations and adjust my night routine (walker within reach, night light, paced transfers); we will review safety after implementation.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 4 Goal: I will keep my feet comfortable and skin/nails well-managed so that my footwear fits better and my wound dressings are easier to apply, with pain generally at or below 4/10 on most days over the next 3 months.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I have bunions and hammertoes (right worse) and frequent dressings. Pain and deformity can make dressings and shoes difficult.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo Allied Health Podiatrist will provide foot care every 6–8 weeks (skin, nails, pressure offloading advice) and liaise with the RN about dressing-friendly footwear and padding; I will check dressings daily and report wetness/pain spikes.

risks.description: History of approximately 10–12 falls in the past year, often when rushing to the bathroom due to urinary urgency; balance issues and tendency to turn too quickly; uses a walker. Has hit head and required CT scans after some falls.
Chronic foot wounds/skin tears with bunions and hammertoes; requires dressings three times weekly. Dressings sometimes become wet, particularly on the left foot.
Constant foot pain affecting sleep and mood; wakes at night. Often sleeps in a chair due to pain.
OCD with dust phobia and high generalized anxiety; past mental breakdown in 1984. Reports increased anger related to stress and pain.
Urinary urgency; uses continence pads. Urgency contributes to rushing and falls on the way to the toilet.
Difficulty getting into cars due to limited right knee flexion post knee replacement; must enter from left side. Balance issues and furniture walking at home.
Mild shortness of breath on inclines.
Allergic reaction to theatre tape/adhesives reported after prior surgery.
Tends to stay indoors and not engage in village activities; worries about visitors seeing a messy kitchen.
Minor stroke in 2010 with residual left-sided hand numbness.
Possible facial skin cancer lesion awaiting specialist review.

medical.allergies: Allergic to theatre tape/adhesive tape. Dust is a phobia (not an allergy).
medical.medications: Self-manages prescribed medicines via blister packs. Takes paracetamol (two tablets every four hours when pain spikes). On a medication for urinary urgency (name not stated). Previously took Lyrica (pregabalin) for nerve pain but ceased due to sleepiness and falls. No patches or injections.

care_analyses.generated_html:
Care Plan

Care Alerts

I have a diagnosed Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) with a phobia of dust; please keep visible surfaces clear and avoid stirring up dust during visits.

I am allergic/sensitive to theatre tape (historical issue post-surgery); avoid using theatre tape on my skin.

I have had 10–12 falls in the past year; I use a walker and have balance issues, especially when rushing to the bathroom due to urinary urgency.

I require wound care/dressings three times per week (currently feet), with the left foot more prone to wet/macerated dressings.

Pain in my feet is constant and can disturb my sleep; I take Panadol as needed (two tablets when pain spikes).

I prefer workers to call triple zero (000) first in an emergency, commence resuscitation (CPR), then call my family.

I accept male or female care workers; please communicate clearly, allow extra time for decisions, and provide reassurance when my anxiety is heightened.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 16 September 2025

Preferred Name: Denise

Full Name: Denise Ruxton

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

  • I, Denise Ruxton, participated in the assessment and co-designed this plan.

  • Care Partner (assessor) facilitated the assessment and planning.

  • Bruce (my husband) contributed during the discussion.

  • Lee (my son and enduring power of attorney) holds my advance care plan and can be consulted as required.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I am Catholic; God and family are very important to me, along with honesty. I would like to be more assertive.

I identify as heterosexual.

I have OCD with a strong phobia of dust. Please be mindful of cleaning approaches and reassurance to reduce anxiety.

At end of life, I would like to speak with a priest or pastoral care representative.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I am comfortable with male or female workers.

Please communicate clearly, give me time to make decisions, and provide gentle prompts to slow down for safety.

Please schedule wound care on Monday/Wednesday/Friday mornings (around 9–10 am) and align with Bruce’s routine where possible to minimise disruption to our day.

Please keep visible surfaces free of dust and clutter to reduce my anxiety; kitchen benches are a particular trigger for me.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination

My Preferred Support People

  • Bruce (husband)

  • Amanda (daughter)

  • Lee (son, enduring power of attorney)

  • Tracey (daughter-in-law)

Informal Supports

Bruce is my primary support at home. We plan to build routines together in our new home in Ballarat, including eating breakfast out every second day.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the second of four sisters and was raised in a Catholic family. I trained as a nurse at St Vincent’s Hospital in Melbourne and worked in nursing for many years, including palliative care and night duty. I also trained in social work and worked with homeless men in North Melbourne before returning to nursing. I married Bruce in 1962; we recently celebrated our 63rd anniversary. I retired around age 59.

Interests

I like getting household tasks done and feel best when I’ve had breakfast early and can get started. I would like to have time to read (e.g., Country Life magazine) and to build more social routines. Going out with Bruce (e.g., breakfast) makes me happy. I want my kitchen to look tidy for visitors.

My Medical Information

Medical History:

  • OCD with phobia of dust; high anxiety/worry.

  • Mental health “breakdown” in 1984; completed an OCD program with some improvement.

  • Right knee replacement (reduced right-leg flexibility).

  • Right mastectomy for large cancer; multiple prior lumpectomies.

  • Minor stroke in 2010 with residual left-sided numbness (fingers feel “wooden”).

  • Foot injuries including three broken bones in the foot (wore a moon boot for 7 weeks), prior broken toe; taxi ran over foot approximately a year ago.

  • Three broken bones in hand (just before last Christmas).

  • Bunions (right worse) and hammertoes (right worse), complicating dressings.

  • Possible facial skin lesion (to be reviewed by skin specialist after move).

  • Shortness of breath on inclines.

Medication:

  • Blister-packed regular medications (names not recorded in this transcript).

  • Bladder urgency medication (name not recorded) to help with urinary urgency.

  • Panadol as needed for pain (typically two tablets when pain spikes; not every day).

  • Lyrica ceased due to sleepiness and increased falls.

Mobility and Equipment:

  • I use a walker; I also “furniture-walk.” Indoor walker use has been recommended.

  • Balance is my main difficulty; I tend to turn too quickly and rush, particularly to the bathroom.

  • I approach car entry from the left side due to right knee limitations.

  • I have an over-toilet aid and use continence pads.

  • I often sleep in a recliner due to pain but want OT help to return to bed sleeping.

GP / Pharmacy: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

CALD: Not identified. Living with disability (mobility): Yes – high falls risk, walker-dependent. Mental health (low mood/isolation risk): Yes – anxiety/OCD and worry.

Specific Risks

  • Falls risk: 10–12 falls in the past year; worsens when rushing to the bathroom due to urinary urgency; balance impairments and quick turns.

  • Wound risk: Left foot dressings can become wet; risk of maceration/infection.

  • Pain-related sleep disturbance leading to fatigue and reduced function; currently sleeping in a chair.

  • Transfer risk: Difficult car entry/exit; right knee limited flexion.

  • Mental health: Anxiety/OCD with dust phobia; cluttered kitchen triggers anxiety.

  • Allergy/sensitivity to theatre tape; avoid use on skin.

  • Breathlessness on inclines; pace activities to avoid overexertion.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

If there is no answer for a scheduled visit: call my mobile, check with neighbours/management, then contact my family. There will be a key available through the office/management.

If I am found unconscious or not breathing during a visit: call triple zero (000) immediately, commence resuscitation (CPR), then call my family.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Registered Nurse to attend Monday/Wednesday/Friday to assess, cleanse and re-dress wounds; monitor exudate, skin condition, and pain; educate me on when to change a wet dressing; liaise with podiatry/GP as needed.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Registered Nurse; I will report wet dressings and pain levels. When will it be done?: Mon/Wed/Fri around 9–10 am for the next 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: RN $148.50/hour x ~12 hours/month ≈ $1,782/month (dressings billed to package as required).

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 2 Goal: I will reduce my falls by building balance and safe walking habits so I have no more than 1 fall in the next 3 months and can complete my home exercise program 5 days/week.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I use a walker, turn too quickly, and rush to the bathroom due to urgency; 10–12 falls in past year.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Allied Health Physiotherapist to review and progress a home exercise and gait training program; practice slow turns, pacing and indoor walker use; consider TUG or similar functional measure at baseline and 12 weeks.

Who is responsible?: Salveo HomeCare Allied Health Therapist (Physio) and me. When will it be done?: 1 hour monthly with daily home practice (5 days/week) over 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Physio $180/hour = $180/month.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 3 Goal: I will safely return to sleeping in my bed (not the chair) at least 5 nights per week within 12 weeks by implementing OT recommendations and transfer strategies.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Pain disturbs sleep; I currently sleep in a recliner; bed transfers feel difficult; risk of pressure and poor rest if I remain in the chair.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Occupational Therapist comprehensive assessment of bed/chair transfers, environment, and equipment needs; teach techniques and stage a graded plan to move back to bed; follow-up to review progress.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can become grumpy/anxious; decision-making can be slow; I benefit from gentle prompts and reassurance.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Weekly Social Support visit to prompt pacing, gentle planning, and brief check-in; create a simple morning checklist; reinforce relaxation strategies taught previously.

The assessment begins with questions about Denise's cultural background, where she reveals she has OCD with a particular phobia of dust. She mentions having experienced a mental breakdown in 1984 and discusses her core values, identifying God and family as most important to her, along with honesty. She expresses a desire to be more assertive. 
Denise provides her Medicare information and confirms she is responsible for making her own decisions, though sometimes she's not quick with them. When discussing end-of-life preferences, she mentions wanting to speak with a priest or pastoral care when the time comes. 
The healthcare worker collects emergency contact information and establishes protocols for scheduled visits, including what to do if Denise is found unconscious (call triple zero, perform resuscitation, and call family). Denise shares that care workers need to know about her OCD and dust phobia, and mentions she has an allergy to theater tape. 
When discussing her daily routine, Denise explains that a good day involves having breakfast early and getting to work on household tasks she wants to accomplish. She identifies anxiety as a significant issue, describing herself as "a worrier." Bad days involve getting up grumpy and experiencing heightened anxiety and OCD symptoms. She acknowledges needing to relax more and appreciates help with household tasks like washing stockings and kitchen cleaning. 
Denise shares her life history, including being the second of four sisters, training as a nurse at St. Vincent's Hospital in Melbourne, getting married at 22, and having children shortly after. She worked as a nurse for many years, took a break due to burnout, pursued social work training, and then returned to nursing, working in palliative care before retiring around age 59. 
The healthcare worker assesses Denise's current health status, noting she experiences constant pain, particularly in her feet, which affects her mobility and sleep. She uses a walker and has had 10-12 falls in the past year. She has had several medical procedures including a right knee replacement, right mastectomy, and broken bones in her hand and foot. She requires wound dressings three times a week and has issues with her feet including bunions and hammertoes. 
The assessment concludes with arrangements for various services including nursing visits for wound care (Monday, Wednesday, Friday), domestic assistance (Thursdays), physiotherapy, occupational therapy assessment, podiatry, meal delivery, and taxi services. Denise describes what keeps her healthy and safe, including taking medications on time, eating well, and trying to drink enough fluids. Denise shares her life history as the second of four sisters in a Catholic family. She trained as a nurse at St. Vincent's Hospital in Melbourne after briefly working in a secretarial job. She retired around age 59 and initially felt a loss when she stopped receiving calls to come in for shifts.

The healthcare worker assesses Denise's current health status. Denise reports experiencing anger due to stress and pain, particularly in her feet. Denise reports constant pain, particularly in her feet, which affects her mobility and sleep. She takes Panadol (two tablets every four hours) when pain spikes but had to stop taking Lyrica due to side effects of sleepiness and falls. 
Mobility Assessment and Fall History ‎ 00:46:01
Denise requires a walker for mobility and identifies balance as her main difficulty, along with turning too quickly and not walking slowly enough. She reports having had 10-12 falls in the past year, with the worst being two falls in one week after New Year's. She mentions that falls often occur when she's rushing to the bathroom due to urinary urgency. Care Plan

Care Alerts

Resuscitation preference: If I am found unconscious or not breathing, call 000 first, commence CPR/resuscitation, then contact my family.

Allergy / adverse reaction: I have a known reaction to theatre/adhesive tape. Use hypoallergenic alternatives and protect my skin when securing dressings.

Mental health and triggers: I live with OCD with a specific phobia of dust. Please keep language calm, avoid minimising my fears, and prioritise low-dust cleaning approaches.

Falls risk: I have had approximately 10–12 falls in the past year. My balance is reduced and rushing to the toilet increases risk. I use a walker and “furniture walk” at times.

Wounds: I have foot wounds requiring dressings three times per week. Monitor for wet dressings between visits (left foot often gets wet) and signs of infection.

Pain: Ongoing foot pain disturbs sleep. I take Panadol (two tablets when pain spikes, up to every 4 hours as needed).

Mobility: Enter cars from the left side due to right knee replacement and limited flexion. Keep my walker within easy reach.

End of life / pastoral care: When appropriate, I would like to speak with a priest or pastoral care person.

Access / welfare checks: If there is no answer at a scheduled visit, call my mobile, check neighbours and village management. There is a key in the office. Then contact my family.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 17 September 2025

Preferred Name: Denise

Full Name: Denise Ruxton

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I developed this plan together with my care partner. My husband Bruce contributed, and my family (Amanda and Lee, and Lee’s wife Tracey) were considered. Lee holds my enduring power of attorney and has my advance care plan.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I identify as a Catholic and God is very important to me. My core values are God, family and honesty. I welcome either male or female workers. I live with OCD, with a specific phobia of dust, and I appreciate care that recognises this. I prefer to be more assertive and I am working on this.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer workers to communicate clearly and calmly, explaining what they will do before they start. Please be mindful of my OCD and dust phobia and help reduce visible dust and clutter in the kitchen area.

Mornings work well (particularly for nursing on Monday, Wednesday and Friday around 9–10am) so I can have the rest of the day free for tasks.

If I do not answer the door for a scheduled visit, please call my mobile, check with neighbours and village management, and note there is a key in the office.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination

My Preferred Support People

My preferred support people are my husband Bruce, my children Amanda and Lee, and my daughter-in-law Tracey. I also value contact with a priest or pastoral care when needed.

Informal Supports

My husband Bruce provides day-to-day support at home. My children (Amanda and Lee) and extended family (including grandchildren and great-grandchildren) are important to me and offer support as they are able.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the second of four sisters and grew up in a Catholic family. I trained as a nurse at St Vincent’s Hospital, Melbourne, married Bruce at 22 (we recently celebrated our 63rd anniversary), and raised our children. I worked many years in nursing (including palliative care and night duty), had a period of burnout and completed social work training, working with homeless men in North Melbourne, then returned to nursing in Tasmania before retiring around age 59.

Interests

I enjoy being with Bruce and family; Bruce smiling makes me happy. I like to keep busy with household tasks and would like to make more time to relax (even to read a magazine). I am looking forward to going out for breakfast with Bruce every second morning in Ballarat.

My Medical Information

Medical History:

I live with OCD (dust phobia) and anxiety. I had a mental health breakdown in 1984. I had a right knee replacement, a right mastectomy for a large cancer after several prior lumpectomies, a minor stroke in 2010 affecting my left side (residual numbness in fingers), and fractures in my hand after a fall. A taxi ran over my foot about a year ago and I wore a moon boot for seven weeks. I have bunions (right worse) and hammertoes, with fragile skin between toes. I have constant foot pain that disturbs my sleep. I experience urinary urgency that contributes to rushing and falls. I may have a skin lesion on my face awaiting dermatology review. I become a little short of breath walking up inclines.

Medication:

I use blister packs. I take Panadol (two tablets up to every 4 hours when pain spikes). I previously used Lyrica but stopped due to sleepiness and falls. I am taking a bladder medication for urinary urgency (name not recorded). I do not require assistance with medications. I have a known reaction to theatre/adhesive tape.

Mobility and Equipment:

I walk with a walker and sometimes furniture-walk. My balance is reduced, especially when turning quickly or rushing. I enter cars from the left side due to limited right knee flexion after knee replacement. I currently sleep in a big chair because of pain and plan an OT assessment to support bed transfers. I have an over-toilet aid and compression stockings that need weekly washing.

GP / Pharmacy: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

If there is no answer at a scheduled visit, call my mobile, check with neighbours and village management. There is a key in the office. Then contact my family (Amanda and Lee).

How will we do this? (Tasks): Salveo Registered Nurse to review wounds, cleanse and redress three times weekly; supply and use hypoallergenic fixation where needed; monitor for infection; educate me to check for wet dressings; coordinate with podiatry; escalate to GP if deterioration occurs.

GOAL 4 Goal: I will reduce my anxiety about dust and visible kitchen clutter by having weekly help focused on kitchen benches, dusting and washing my compression stockings so visitors see a tidy space each week over the next 3 months.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I experience OCD with a dust phobia and worry about the kitchen being cluttered. Standing too long increases pain and fatigue.

Who is responsible?: Me and Salveo Domestic Assistance worker. When will it be done?: 2 hours weekly on Thursdays. How much will it cost?: Domestic Assistance $85/hour, 2 hours/week ≈ 8.66 hours/month ≈ $736.10/month.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can report pain and pressure areas. Risks include fragile skin between toes and footwear issues while wounds are draining.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Allied Health Podiatrist home visit 1 hour every 6–8 weeks for skin/nail care, pressure management advice, and liaison with nursing on dressings and footwear advice.

Who is responsible?: Me and Salveo Allied Health Therapist (Podiatry). When will it be done?: 1 hour every 6–8 weeks. How much will it cost?: Allied Health Therapist $180/hour, monthly equivalent ≈ $97.43–$129.91 (depending on 6–8 week cycle).

Service Category: Clinical Care

Budget and Service Classifications

Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded) / Independence Support / Everyday Living

  • Registered Nurse wound care: Clinical Care – $1,930.50/month (≈$5,791.50 per quarter).

Care Plan

Care Alerts

I have Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) with a specific phobia of dust (fear, not allergy). Please minimise dust exposure and explain any cleaning or rearrangement before starting.

I am allergic to theatre tape (adhesive); please avoid adhesive tapes for dressings where possible and use skin-friendly alternatives.

I am at high risk of falls (10–12 falls over the past year), particularly when rushing to the bathroom due to urinary urgency. I use a walker and have balance issues, especially when turning quickly.

I require wound care to my feet/legs with dressings three times per week (Monday/Wednesday/Friday).

Emergency preference: call triple zero (000), commence resuscitation (CPR), then call my family.

I have residual numbness in my left hand/fingers following a minor stroke (2010), which may impact sensation and safety with hot/cold and fine tasks.

I experience constant foot pain that affects sleep and mobility.

I enter cars from the left side only due to limited right knee flexion following right total knee replacement.

I currently sleep mostly in a chair; I want Occupational Therapy support to safely return to bed.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 17 September 2025

Preferred Name: Denise

Full Name: Denise Ruxton

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I developed this plan together with my care partner/assessor, my husband Bruce, and my family (children Amanda and Lee, and Lee’s wife Tracey). Lee holds my enduring power of attorney and has my advance care plan documents.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I am Catholic and God is very important to me. My core values are faith, family, honesty and becoming more assertive. I am heterosexual. I am comfortable with either male or female workers. When I am at end of life, I would like to talk with a priest or a pastoral care person.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

Please be aware of and respectful towards my OCD and dust phobia. Explain cleaning tasks before you start and avoid creating visible dust. Reassure me and check in if I appear anxious.

Please avoid using theatre tape or strong adhesives on my skin. Use alternatives for dressings.

If I do not answer at a scheduled visit: call my mobile, check with neighbours/retirement village management, and then call family. There will be a key in the office for access if required.

For emergencies during visits: call triple zero (000) first, commence resuscitation (CPR), then call my family.

I prefer morning routines that help me have breakfast early, so I can get on with the day’s tasks.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination.

My Preferred Support People

My husband Bruce is my primary support person. My children Amanda and Lee (and Lee’s wife Tracey) are my key family supports. I also value my grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

Informal Supports

Bruce provides day-to-day support and companionship at home. Family provide emotional support and contact.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the second of four sisters in a Catholic family. I trained and worked as a nurse (St Vincent’s Hospital, Melbourne) and later completed social work training, working with homeless men in North Melbourne. I returned to nursing in Tasmania, including palliative care (often nights), and retired around age 59. Bruce and I married in 1962 and recently celebrated 63 years together.

Interests

Bruce’s happiness makes me happy (“Bruce smiling”). I enjoy family time with my children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. I want to make space again for simple pleasures like reading. We plan to go out for breakfast together regularly in Ballarat. We have one cat.

Medical History:

OCD with dust phobia; mental health breakdown in 1984 (historical). Right knee replacement (limited flexion persists). Right mastectomy for cancer after multiple lumpectomies. Minor stroke in 2010 with residual numbness on the left side (fingers). Multiple falls, including fractures of hand bones (pre-Christmas) and a prior broken toe. Foot injury about a year ago (taxi ran over foot) requiring a moon boot for seven weeks. Foot problems include bunions (right worse) and hammertoes. Possible facial skin cancer pending dermatology review. Shortness of breath on inclines. Constant foot pain affecting sleep and function. No diagnosis of dementia; I have noted normal age-related cognitive changes.

Medication:

I use blister packs and manage my own medicines. I take paracetamol (two tablets every four hours as needed) for pain flares (not every day). I previously trialled pregabalin (Lyrica) but ceased due to sleepiness and increased falls. I take a medication aimed at bladder urgency (name not recorded in this transcript). I do not require help with patches, injections or blood glucose monitoring.

Mobility and Equipment:

I use a walker and sometimes furniture-walk at home (I have been advised to use the walker indoors). I have balance difficulties and fall risk, particularly when rushing to the toilet. I approach car transfers from the left side only due to right knee limitations. I have an over-toilet aid/appliance. I wear stockings (compression/hosiery) that need washing support. I currently sleep mostly in a chair and want to resume sleeping in bed with OT support and equipment as advised.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I can trial positioning strategies with guidance. Risks include night-time pain, urgency to toilet, and falls when getting up.

risks.description: Limited mobility; uses stick/walker/wheelchair. One fall in past 18 months (slipped off bed) and a prior fall 2–3 years ago (slipped on concrete chasing cat). Geriatrician has classified her as frail.
COPD with shortness of breath, especially after showering; uses maintenance inhaler and Ventolin PRN.
Bruises and skin tears easily due to blood thinners; moisturiser (QV) used to manage dryness; occasional nose-picking causes minor wounds.
Alzheimer’s-related anxiety, particularly when feeling alone; background trauma from Stolen Generation; anxiety currently helped by medication.
Ongoing weight loss (~78 kg) and under dietitian review.
Cat in home (consider worker allergies); garden hazard previously addressed by levelling.
Occasional back pain managed with Panadeine Osteo and rest/heat pack.

Care Plan

Care Alerts

Allergies: I am allergic to aspirin and Norspan (buprenorphine) patches.

Advanced Care Directive: I have an Advance Care Directive with clear wishes of no resuscitation and no life support/intubation. A copy is to be provided to the provider and kept readily available in my home and on my file.

Emergency Protocol: In a medical emergency, call 000, do not perform CPR on me, and contact my family (call my grandson first, then my son).

Medications: My medicines are dispensed in pharmacy blister packs. I take Panadeine Osteo (two in the morning and two before bed) for back pain; I use a regular preventer puffer (two puffs morning and night) and Ventolin as needed, especially around showering.

Bleeding/Skin: I bruise and tear easily (likely related to blood thinners). Handle my skin with care and moisturise regularly.

Cognition/Communication: I live with Alzheimer’s disease. Please speak slowly, be patient, and be prepared to repeat questions. Anxiety can increase if I feel alone.

Falls/Mobility: I have limited mobility and am at risk of falls. I use a walking stick inside (sometimes I forget it), a 4WW for longer distances, and a wheelchair for extended outings.

Breathlessness: I have COPD and can become short of breath after showering or exertion.

Home environment: I have a cat in the home. Please only send workers who are comfortable with pets.

Worker preference: I prefer female support workers.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 7 October 2025

Preferred Name: Anne

Full Name: Anne Martin

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I developed this plan with my care partner and my grandson (Ioanides), who is my primary caregiver and lives with me. My son Brett was consulted as a secondary contact. This plan reflects my wishes and the information we discussed together.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I identify as an Aboriginal woman (approximately 50%) and I am part of the Stolen Generation. This history can sometimes trigger anxiety, especially fears about losing my home. Please be trauma-informed, respectful, and keep me well informed about any changes.

I value honesty, punctuality, and good communication. My family and I are “go with the flow” people—as long as we are kept informed about any changes. I have no specific religious practices and no preference about workers’ cultural backgrounds; I do prefer female workers.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer female support workers who are patient, speak slowly and clearly, and are comfortable repeating information when needed.

I prefer services to occur before 2:00 PM. I appreciate punctuality and a quick call or message if a worker is running late or there is a change.

Please ensure workers are comfortable with my cat and keep doors and pathways clear.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination

My Preferred Support People

My preferred support people are my grandson (Ioanides) as my primary caregiver and my son Brett. I also value support from Mary Lou, Manet (Darren Peachy), and my health service team.

Informal Supports

I live with my grandson, who supports me day-to-day, coordinates appointments, and helps me plan my day to reduce fatigue. My son Brett also supports me, and my daughter-in-law lives 10 minutes away and can help in emergencies. My family provides transport and companionship, and helps collect my blister packs from the pharmacy.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I was born in Mildura and lived on the Murray River when I was young before being taken as part of the Stolen Generation and placed in a girls’ home in Brighton. I married young and had three children. I worked in many roles including bookbinder, cleaner, drug and alcohol counsellor, emergency housing services officer, and at sobering-up houses—giving back to the community for much of my adult life.

Interests

I like to be busy. I enjoy playing bingo at my own pace at home, gentle ball exercises, going shopping, and going out for coffee with family. I enjoy time with my family and my cat. A good day is when I have something to look forward to; a bad day is when I have back pain and feel very tired.

My Medical Information

Medical History: Alzheimer’s disease (PET-confirmed), COPD, back pain, easy bruising/skin tears, ongoing weight loss with dietitian involvement. I have been described as “frail” by my geriatrician due to tiredness and walking independence issues. I sometimes experience anxiety related to Alzheimer’s, especially if I feel alone.

Medication: Pharmacy blister packs. Panadeine Osteo two tablets in the morning and two before bed for back pain. Preventer inhaler two puffs morning and night; Ventolin as needed (often around showering). Moisturisers (e.g., QV) for skin; occasional Bepanthen or low-dose hydrocortisone on skin picking areas as directed by my GP.

Allergies: Aspirin; Norspan patches.

Mobility and Equipment: I have a walking stick (inside), a 4-wheel walker for longer distances, and a wheelchair for extended outings. I use an adjustable (hospital-style) bed and an over-bed table. I have a shower chair and stool, raised toilet seat, and handrails throughout the home. I use an “easy bar” for car transfers. I sometimes forget my stick indoors and “furniture surf.”

GP / Pharmacy: GP: Victorian Aboriginal Health Service (VAHS), South Morang (855 Plenty Road). Current GP: Dr Kieran Shields (covering while my usual GP is on maternity leave). Pharmacy: TerryWhite Chemist, Mill Park Lakes (dispenses blister packs).

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):) CALD: I am an Aboriginal woman and part of the Stolen Generation; English-speaking. Living with disability (mobility): Limited mobility; fall risk; use multiple mobility aids. Mental health: Risk of anxiety if I feel alone; risk of low mood if fatigued or in pain.

Specific Risks

Falls risk due to limited mobility and fatigue; previous slip off the bed (18 months ago) and a fall chasing my cat (2–3 years ago).

Breathlessness around showering or exertion due to COPD.

Skin tears and bruising easily; minor skin picking when bored or in sleep.

Anxiety related to Alzheimer’s, especially when I feel alone or after naps.

Occasional back pain that can limit activity and sleep.

No personal alarm currently; however, I live with family and have a grab-and-go emergency bag.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

In an emergency: Call 000. Do not perform CPR. Respect my Advance Care Directive. Then contact my family—call my grandson (primary) first, then my son Brett. If a worker arrives for a scheduled visit and cannot get a response, call my grandson first, then Brett.

Emergency preparation: I keep a medical emergency bag ready (clothing and toiletries). I have strong family support close by.

Contact details: Names and call order are documented above; specific phone numbers were discussed but not fully captured.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will shower safely and feel less breathless, with hair washed weekly and dressing supported after showers, so that I can enjoy more “good days” without feeling worn out.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I have COPD (breathless after shower), Alzheimer’s (need patience/repetition), easy bruising/skin tears, and limited mobility with falls risk.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Use my shower chair and rails; have a female support worker assist three mornings a week (Mon/Wed/Fri 10–11 AM); use Ventolin as needed before/after shower; complete the shower within ~30 minutes; weekly hair wash; dress with support; rest and hydrate after; document any breathlessness or skin issues.

Who is responsible?: I am, supported by your provider’s Personal Care workers and my grandson. When will it be done?: 3 times weekly, before 2 PM, over the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Personal Care 3 hrs/week at $85/hour ≈ 12.99 hrs/month = $1104.15/month.

Service Category: Independence Support

GOAL 2 Goal: I will keep my home clean and safe so I can move around without trip hazards and feel comfortable having visitors.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I fatigue easily and have a falls risk; I benefit from help with heavier or time-consuming tasks.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Weekly Domestic Assistance on Mondays 11 AM–12 PM for kitchen and bathroom clean, dusting, vacuum/mop of high-traffic areas, laundry/linen change as needed, and clearing walkways.

Who is responsible?: I am, supported by your provider’s Domestic Assistance worker and my grandson. When will it be done?: 1 hour weekly for the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: 1 hr/week at $85/hour ≈ 4.33 hrs/month = $368.05/month.

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 3 Goal: I will get out for coffee/shopping and meaningful activities at least 7 times per month so I feel connected and less alone.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I like to be busy but tire easily; anxiety increases if I feel alone; I need my walker or wheelchair for distance.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Social Support with a female worker on Wednesdays and Fridays 11 AM–12 PM; plan simple outings (coffee, short shop, bingo at my pace at home if I’m fatigued); use wheelchair for longer distances; pace and rest; log outings and mood.

Who is responsible?: I am, supported by your provider’s Social Support workers and my family. When will it be done?: 2 hours weekly for the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Social Support 2 hrs/week at $85/hour ≈ 8.66 hrs/month = $736.10/month, plus transport at $1.40/km (billed per actual travel).

Service Category: Independence Support

GOAL 4 Goal: I will improve my strength and balance so I can walk safely with my walker at home and reduce my risk of falls.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I have limited mobility, sometimes forget my stick, and tire easily; I have had rare falls.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Allied Health Physiotherapy 1 hour fortnightly (female physiotherapist) to review gait and balance and set a home exercise program; I will complete my prescribed exercises at least 5 days/week (10–15 minutes), and use my stick/walker consistently; workers will prompt safe technique.

Who is responsible?: I am, with your provider’s Allied Health Therapist (Physiotherapist), support workers, and my grandson. When will it be done?: Fortnightly physiotherapy over the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Physio 1 hr/fortnight at $180/hour ≈ $360/month.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 5 Goal: I will maintain comfortable feet and prevent cracked skin/tinea so walking is safer and more comfortable.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Dry, cracked skin and occasional tinea increase discomfort and falls risk; I bruise/tear easily.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Podiatry through Stellar for 1 hour every other month; follow foot care regime (moisturiser, socks/footwear guidance); workers to observe/report skin issues; keep floors clear.

Who is responsible?: I am, with your provider arranging Podiatry and my support workers. When will it be done?: One hour every other month for the next quarter (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Podiatry budgeted at $180/hour every 2 months ≈ $90/month.

Service Category: Clinical Care

Budget and Service Classifications

Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded) / Independence Support / Everyday Living

Quarterly Budget Allocation

Independence Support:

  • Personal Care: ≈ 12.99 hrs/month x $85 = $1104.15/month
  • Social Support: ≈ 8.66 hrs/month x $85 = $736.10/month (+ transport $1.40/km as used)

Everyday Living:

  • Domestic Assistance: ≈ 4.33 hrs/month x $85 = $368.05/month

Clinical Care:

  • Physiotherapy: 1 hr/fortnight ≈ $360/month
  • Podiatry: 1 hr every other month ≈ $90/month

Estimated total monthly (excluding km): $1104.15 + $736.10 + $368.05 + $360 + $90 = $2658.30/month.

Estimated total quarterly (3 months, excluding km): $7974.90.

Transport will be billed at $1.40/km for community outings; actual kilometers will be logged per visit and added to the above.

Classification Level (1-8 under Support at Home): Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Care Plan Consent and Distribution

I have been involved in developing this plan and agree to the goals, services, and preferences described. I consent to share this plan with my provider, my nominated family supports (grandson and son), and my GP as needed for safe care coordination. My Advance Care Directive will be attached to my record when received.

Prepared By (Name: __________ | Role: Care Partner, Date: Today | Review Date: Quarterly (every 3 months) | Signature: __________)

Transcript Summary – Anne Martin (map to Standards 1–8)

Standard 1 – Consumer dignity and choice: I stated my preferences for female workers, punctuality, clear communication, and trauma-informed respect for my background as an Aboriginal woman from the Stolen Generation. I prefer services before 2 PM and want to be kept informed of any changes.

Standard 2 – Ongoing assessment and planning with consumers: My assessment covered health (Alzheimer’s, COPD, pain), mobility, equipment, home environment, risks, and social needs. My family and I co-designed goals with clear frequencies and review quarterly. My Advance Care Directive (DNR) will be attached.

Standard 3 – Personal care and clinical care: Personal Care is scheduled 3x weekly with COPD precautions. Clinical supports include physiotherapy fortnightly and podiatry bi-monthly. Allergies, skin fragility, and breathlessness were documented with mitigation strategies.

Standard 4 – Services and supports for daily living: Domestic Assistance weekly maintains a safe, clean environment. Social Support twice weekly helps me stay active and connected, including paced bingo at home or short community outings.

Standard 5 – Organisation's service environment: My home has handrails, shower chair, raised toilet seat, and a clear plan to keep pathways free of hazards. Workers will be comfortable with my cat and use safe techniques with my equipment.

Standards 6–8 – Feedback & complaints; Human resources; Organisational governance: I want honest, punctual communication. I understand how to raise concerns through my provider. Staff assigned will meet my gender preference and be trained to support dementia, COPD, and manual handling. The provider will maintain records, safeguard my Advance Care Directive, and review this plan quarterly.

Dignity of Risk Assessment (Narrative + Table)

I choose to live a full life with community outings and meaningful activities, balanced with my health conditions and risks. I accept reasonable risks (for example, going out when I may tire, showering despite possible breathlessness) and agree to mitigation strategies so I can keep doing what matters to me. Summary 
The meeting transcript documents an intake assessment for a home care package for Greg (Gregorias), an elderly Greek man. The assessment was conducted with Greg and his family members present, including his daughter Dimmy and son Elias. The meeting focused on gathering personal information, medical history, care needs, and preferences to establish appropriate home care services. 
Greg was born in Greece and came to Australia in 1960. He speaks English as his second language but communicates effectively. He identifies as Greek Orthodox but doesn't attend religious services. Greg values independence and family, and doesn't have any specific cultural factors that need consideration when matching him with care workers. 
The assessment revealed that Greg has several health conditions including a pacemaker (installed last year), scoliosis, a dropped foot from a back operation, and nerve pain/pins and needles from the waist down. He experiences occasional but severe pain (rated 7/10) that impacts his lifestyle, keeping him awake and limiting his activities. Greg takes medication for pain management including Lyrica, but reports it doesn't provide much relief. 
Greg has limited mobility and is very unsteady on his feet. He has a foot brace but doesn't wear it regularly. He needs assistance when walking and is at high risk of falls. The family expressed concern about his balance issues and mentioned they always hold him when going out to prevent falls. Greg doesn't currently use any walking aids but the assessor recommended an Occupational Therapy (OT) assessment to evaluate his needs for mobility equipment. 
The assessment also covered Greg's daily activities and preferences. He enjoys going to the pool for exercise and socializing, watching sports (especially soccer), and spending time with family. He previously enjoyed fishing and playing backgammon but can no longer do these activities. His family mentioned that he tends to sleep during the day and needs more mental stimulation. 
The care plan established includes: 
•	Social support/transport: Two 3-hour sessions weekly (Tuesdays and Thursdays at 9:00 AM) to take Greg to the pool 
•	Home gardening: 2 hours every three weeks with a professional gardener named Daniel 
•	OT assessment: Up to 3 hours to evaluate equipment needs and home modifications 
•	Continence aids: $25 monthly allowance 
•	Personal alarm: Annual cost coverage 
The assessor also discussed upcoming changes to equipment budgets starting November 1st, explaining that clients will have access to funds (potentially up to $15,000) for equipment purchases based on their assessed level. This could include beds, walking aids, shower chairs, and home modifications. 
The family expressed interest in getting walking aids for Greg and potentially exploring other equipment options following the OT assessment. The assessor emphasized that the goal is to keep Greg active, provide appropriate support for his mobility issues, and increase mental stimulation to improve his quality of life.

Personal Information and Background ‎ 00:00:00

Health Conditions and Mobility ‎ 00:12:07

The family mentioned concerns about his balance and risk of falls. Greg also has memory issues. The assessor recommended an Occupational Therapy (OT) assessment to evaluate his needs for mobility equipment. He has had three collapsed ribs discovered during a CT scan, which contributes to his pain. 
Daily Activities and Quality of Life ‎ 00:14:53
The discussion moved to Greg's daily activities and quality of life. A good day for Greg involves going to the pool for exercise, seeing his grandchildren or other family members, and not experiencing pins and needles. A bad day involves not sleeping through the night and experiencing pins and needles. Greg enjoys watching sports (especially soccer), swimming, and spending time with family. He previously enjoyed fishing and playing backgammon but can no longer do these activities. His family mentioned that he tends to sleep during the day and needs more mental stimulation. They play Uno together as a family activity. 
Life History ‎ 00:26:16
Greg shared details about his life history. He has two brothers and one sister, being the third child in his family. He came to Australia in 1960 and initially worked at General Motors. He was a stonemason in Greece and became a bricklayer in Australia after attending school. He later had his own construction business building houses and commercial properties, which he ran until around 1990. Greg has two children and multiple grandchildren but no great-grandchildren yet. 
Pain Management and Medication ‎ 00:38:30
The assessment covered Greg's pain management and medication needs. Greg experiences occasional but severe pain (rated 7/10) that impacts his lifestyle, keeping him awake and limiting his activities. The pain comes randomly and doesn't seem to have specific triggers. Greg takes medication for pain management including Lyrica and paracetamol, but reports they don't provide much relief. His wife currently manages his medications. Greg also takes medication for blood pressure and recently started taking Mirtazapine to help with sleep. 
Personal Care and Equipment Needs ‎ 00:44:45
The assessor discussed Greg's personal care needs and current equipment. Greg has a shower chair, raised toilet seat, recliner chair, and a brace for his foot/leg. He needs assistance with changing clothes when going to the pool but can shower independently. He needs help with drying his back and getting dressed. Greg doesn't need assistance with oral care and has his own teeth. He visits the dentist every six months. Greg experiences itching after swimming in the pool, likely due to chlorine, and uses QV skin products. He has issues with his toe that may require podiatry services. 
Continence and Dietary Requirements ‎ 00:53:36
Greg uses continence aids at night as a precaution, wearing them about three nights per week. The family spends approximately $25 per month on these products. The assessor offered to reimburse these expenses through the care package. Greg has a good appetite but has an unusual reaction to sweets and sugar, which taste bitter to him. This is a family trait shared with his sister. Otherwise, Greg has no special dietary requirements. 
Care Plan and Services ‎ 00:57:22
The assessor established a care plan with specific services for Greg. This includes social support/transport for two 3-hour sessions weekly (Tuesdays and Thursdays at 9:00 AM) to take Greg to the pool. Home gardening services will be provided by Daniel (a professional gardener) for 2 hours every three weeks. The plan also includes an OT assessment (up to 3 hours) to evaluate equipment needs and home modifications. Additionally, the package will cover continence aids ($25 monthly) and the annual cost of Greg's personal alarm. The assessor also mentioned that gutter cleaning is available twice a year when needed. 
Equipment Budget and Future Planning ‎ 01:02:24
The assessor discussed upcoming changes to equipment budgets starting November 1st. Clients will have access to funds for equipment purchases based on their assessed level, potentially ranging from $500 to $15,000. This could include beds, walking aids, shower chairs, toilet chairs, handrails, scooters, and other medical equipment. The family expressed interest in getting walking aids for Greg and potentially exploring other equipment options following the OT assessment. The assessor emphasized that the OT would provide recommendations, and they could proceed with purchases once the new equipment budget system is implemented. 
Action Items 
Assessor to arrange OT assessment (2-3 hours) for Greg to evaluate his mobility needs and recommend appropriate walking aids. ‎ 00:12:59
Assessor to schedule social support/transport for Greg twice weekly (Tuesdays and Thursdays at 9:00 AM) to take him to the pool. ‎ 00:57:22

Assessor to push for a level increase for Greg's care package to provide more support. ‎ 00:21:01
Assessor to provide information about the new equipment budget system starting November 1st once details are available. ‎ 01:02:24
Family to consider podiatry services for Greg's toe issues. ‎ 00:48:44

care_analyses.generated_html:
Care Plan

Care Alerts

I have a pacemaker (implanted last year).

I am very unsteady on my feet with a history of near-falls and one recent missed step; I am at high risk of falls due to scoliosis and a dropped foot after back surgery.

I experience severe episodic neuropathic pain (pins and needles from the waist down), rated up to 7/10, which disrupts sleep and daily function.

I have memory issues; please communicate clearly, allow time, and confirm understanding.

I have a Live Life personal alarm; my family reports I rarely use it. Please prompt me to wear it and test it.

Chlorinated pools cause skin itching; I use QV skin products after swimming.

Sweets and sugar taste bitter to me (family trait). I have no known medication allergies documented.

Emergency preference: call 000, commence resuscitation, and call my family. If there is no response at a scheduled visit, call my family first.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 07 October 2025

Preferred Name: Greg

Full Name: Gregirious

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: Greek (I also speak English and communicate effectively)

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I participated in this assessment with my daughter Dimmy (primary contact) and my son Elias. A care partner completed the assessment with us. I agree to involve an Occupational Therapist for a mobility and home safety assessment. A professional gardener named Daniel will provide gardening services.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I was born in Greece and came to Australia in 1960. I am Greek Orthodox but I do not attend religious services. Independence and family are very important to me. I do not have any specific cultural matching requirements for care workers at this time.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I speak English as my second language and communicate well without an interpreter.

I am very unsteady; please provide close standby assistance, ensure safe transfers in and out of the car, and walk within arm’s reach, especially on stairs and wet surfaces at the pool.

Be flexible with scheduling if I have had a rough night; my family may request to delay or switch a pool visit to an at-home social activity session.

If I do not answer the door for a scheduled visit, please call my family first.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination.

My Preferred Support People

My preferred support people are my daughter Dimmy (primary contact) and my son Elias. I also have a sister who lives nearby and close friends.

Informal Supports

My wife manages my medications and accompanies me to the pool. My family provides transport at times, supports me during outings by holding me to prevent falls, visits me regularly, and plays games (e.g., Uno) to keep me mentally stimulated.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the third child in my family (two brothers and one sister). I arrived in Australia in 1960. I worked at General Motors, trained at school here, and became a bricklayer (stonemason in Greece). I later ran my own construction business building houses and commercial properties until around 1990. I have two children and several grandchildren.

Interests

A good day for me is going to the pool, seeing my grandchildren and other family, and having fewer pins and needles. I enjoy watching sports, especially soccer, and talking with friends. I used to enjoy fishing and playing backgammon but I no longer do those activities. I tend to nap during the day and benefit from more mental stimulation (e.g., playing Uno together).

My Medical Information

Medical History

I have a pacemaker (implanted last year), scoliosis, a dropped foot following a back operation, and neuropathic pain with pins and needles from the waist down. A CT scan found three collapsed ribs, which contribute to pain. I have balance issues and memory issues. I do not have documented medication allergies. Sweets and sugar taste bitter to me.

Medication

I take Lyrica (pregabalin) for nerve pain and paracetamol as needed, although these provide limited relief.

I take blood pressure medication.

I recently started mirtazapine at night to help with sleep.

My wife gives me my medications and arranges my medicines.

Mobility and Equipment

My mobility is limited. I am very unsteady and at high risk of falls. I do not currently use a walking aid; I have a brace for my foot/leg but I do not wear it regularly. I have a shower chair, raised toilet seat, handrails in the bathroom, and a recliner chair. I shower independently but need help drying my back and getting dressed after the pool.

GP / Pharmacy

My GP is Dr Lillian Risk, Donvale Medical Centre.

My pharmacy is Terry White, 274 Blackburn Road, Doncaster East.

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

CALD: Yes – I am Greek-born and English is my second language (no interpreter required).

Living with disability (mobility): Yes – high falls risk due to dropped foot and scoliosis; very unsteady on feet.

Mental health (low mood/isolation risk): Yes – I nap a lot during the day and need more stimulation; pain and poor sleep can affect my mood; I have memory issues.

Specific Risks

  • Falls risk at home, on steps, and in community settings (including wet areas at the pool).
  • Episodic severe neuropathic pain (up to 7/10) that impacts sleep and function.
  • Use of sedating medications at night (mirtazapine) may increase morning drowsiness and falls risk.
  • Skin irritation from chlorine after swimming.
  • Toe/foot problems requiring podiatry attention.
  • Pacemaker in situ – avoid strong electromagnetic fields and report any cardiac symptoms promptly.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

Primary contact: Dimmy (daughter). Phone: 0402 201 074.

Secondary contact: Elias (son). Phone: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Personal alarm: Live Life device (annual fee covered by provider). Please encourage me to wear it and test monthly.

No key lockbox at home. Family provides local support.

If I do not respond for a scheduled visit: call my family first.

Medical emergency while care is being provided: call 000, commence resuscitation, and call my family.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will keep active and connected by going to the pool with support every Tuesday and Thursday at 9:00 AM for exercise and to see friends over the next 12 weeks, while staying safe on my feet.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I am very unsteady with a dropped foot and scoliosis; wet areas increase falls risk; chlorine causes skin itching; pain and poor sleep can make mornings difficult.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Your support worker will provide transport, walk within arm’s reach for balance, assist me to change before/after the pool, monitor for fatigue/pain, and prompt QV skin care after swimming. Sessions can be delayed or switched to an at‑home social session if I have had a rough night.

Who is responsible?: Me, my support worker, and my family. When will it be done?: 3 hours per session, twice weekly (Tuesdays and Thursdays at 9:00 AM) for 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Social Support/Transport $85/hour x 6 hours/week x 4 weeks = $2,040/month, plus $1.40/km travel (as incurred).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 2 Goal: I will reduce my risk of falls by completing an Occupational Therapy assessment and starting the recommended walking aid/home safety strategies within 8 weeks, and I will wear my foot brace whenever I leave home.

Abilities and considerations (risks): High falls risk; I have been reluctant to use aids but agree to trial a walking stick or other device; memory issues may affect carryover of strategies.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Arrange an OT home visit (up to 3 hours) to assess mobility, recommend and fit a walking aid, and advise on home modifications; practice 15 minutes of safe gait daily with the aid; family/support worker to cue brace use and safe technique.

Who is responsible?: Me, OT, support worker, and family. When will it be done?: OT visit completed within 4 weeks; aid trial and daily practice commenced by week 6; brace used on all outings by week 8. How much will it cost?: Allied Health Therapist (OT) $180/hour x up to 3 hours = up to $540 once this quarter (equipment to be funded via Support at Home equipment budget when available).

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 3 Goal: I will increase my mental stimulation by using one support session each week for social/cognitive activities at home (e.g., Uno, conversations about soccer, or visiting my sister/friends) when I cannot attend the pool, aiming to reduce daytime naps before 4 PM by 25% over 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Memory issues and variable sleep/pain; I enjoy family time, games, and sports talk which help me stay engaged.

How will we do this? (Tasks): On rough mornings, switch a scheduled pool session to an at‑home social visit; use structured activities (games, photo/music reminiscence, short walks with standby assist) and record activities completed.

Who is responsible?: Me, my support worker, and family. When will it be done?: Up to 3 hours weekly within the existing schedule over 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Reallocated within GOAL 1 Social Support/Transport hours ($0 additional per month).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 4 Goal: I will keep my garden safe and tidy to reduce outdoor trip hazards and maintain pride in my home, with Daniel (professional gardener) attending for 2 hours every 3 weeks over the next 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I am at risk of tripping on uneven pathways and overgrowth; I cannot safely perform pruning or ladder work.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Daniel will prune, tidy paths, and remove trip hazards; family and I will identify priorities before each visit.

Who is responsible?: Gardener (Daniel), me, and my family. When will it be done?: 2 hours every 3 weeks for 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Light Home & Gardening Maintenance $85/hour; approximately 2 hours every 3 weeks ≈ $227/month (average).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 5 Goal: I will address toe discomfort and maintain healthy feet by continuing podiatry via my GP plan and, if needed, adding one in‑home top‑up podiatry visit this quarter to review nails/skin and footwear.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Overlapping toes/thick nails can cause pain and affect balance; mobility issues increase falls risk.

How will we do this? (Tasks): I will attend my usual podiatry; my GP will provide a care plan; if clinically needed, the provider will arrange one in‑home podiatry session and share advice with my family and support workers.

Who is responsible?: Me, my GP, podiatrist, and care partner. When will it be done?: Within 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Allied Health Therapist (Podiatry) $180/hour x 1 once this quarter if required (≈ $60/month averaged across the quarter). GP‑funded sessions billed separately under Medicare.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 6 Goal: I will maintain dignity and comfort overnight by using continence pads as needed (about three nights per week) with reimbursement of approximately $25/month and by tracking dry nights over the next 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Occasional night-time use only; need to ensure correct product and supply.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Purchase pads from the chemist; send receipts for reimbursement; review product/fit as needed.

Who is responsible?: Me and my family. When will it be done?: Ongoing over 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Consumables reimbursement approximately $25/month.

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 7 Goal: I will keep my personal alarm active and test it monthly so I can call for help if I fall or feel unwell.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I rarely use/wear the alarm despite a high falls risk.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Family will prompt me to wear the device daily; the provider will cover the annual fee; we will complete and record a monthly test call.

Who is responsible?: Me, my family, and the care partner. When will it be done?: Test monthly for the next 12 weeks (and ongoing). How much will it cost?: Annual fee approximately $70 covered by provider (≈ $6/month averaged).

Service Category: Everyday Living

Budget and Service Classifications

Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded) / Independence Support / Everyday Living

  • Social Support/Transport to pool and/or at-home social visits: Everyday Living – $2,040/month (6 hours/week at $85/hour) plus $1.40/km travel as incurred.
  • Light Home & Gardening Maintenance (Daniel): Everyday Living – approximately $227/month (2 hours every 3 weeks at $85/hour).
  • Occupational Therapy assessment (up to 3 hours once this quarter): Clinical Care – up to $540 once (Allied Health $180/hour).
  • Podiatry top-up (if required; one in-home session this quarter): Clinical Care – $180 once (Allied Health $180/hour), noting GP-plan sessions are billed separately.
  • Continence aids: Everyday Living – approximately $25/month (reimbursement upon receipts).
  • Personal alarm annual fee: Everyday Living – approximately $70/year (≈ $6/month averaged), covered by provider when due.

Quarterly Budget Allocation

  • Social Support/Transport: ≈ $2,040 x 3 = $6,120 (plus kilometres as incurred).
  • Gardening: ≈ $227 x 3 = $681.
  • OT assessment: up to $540 (once this quarter).
  • Podiatry top-up (if required): $180 (once this quarter).
  • Continence aids: ≈ $25 x 3 = $75.
  • Personal alarm: ≈ $6 x 3 = $18 (averaged; actual charge when renewal falls due).

Classification Level (1-8 under Support at Home): Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Transcript Summary – Gregirious (map to Standards 1–8)

Standard 1 – Consumer dignity and choice: I stated that independence and family are important to me. I chose to continue pool visits for exercise and social connection and agreed to trial a walking aid after an OT assessment. I do not require an interpreter and have no cultural matching preferences for workers.

Standard 2 – Ongoing assessment and planning with consumers: The assessment covered my health, mobility, pain, daily living, preferences, and risks. An OT assessment (up to 3 hours) will further evaluate mobility equipment and home safety. My plan will be reviewed quarterly.

Standard 3 – Personal care and clinical care: I shower independently and need help with drying/dressing after the pool. My medications are managed by my wife; I recently started mirtazapine. Pain is managed with Lyrica and paracetamol (limited benefit). Clinical supports include OT and podiatry (as needed). My pacemaker is noted.

I agree to trial a walking aid and to wear my foot brace when I go out. I acknowledge my personal alarm helps me call for assistance and agree to wear and test it regularly.
