Care Plan

Care Alerts

Allergies: I am allergic to aspirin and Norspan (buprenorphine) patches.

Advanced Care Directive: I have an Advance Care Directive with clear wishes of no resuscitation and no life support/intubation. A copy is to be provided to the provider and kept readily available in my home and on my file.

Emergency Protocol: In a medical emergency, call 000, do not perform CPR on me, and contact my family (call my grandson first, then my son).

Medications: My medicines are dispensed in pharmacy blister packs. I take Panadeine Osteo (two in the morning and two before bed) for back pain; I use a regular preventer puffer (two puffs morning and night) and Ventolin as needed, especially around showering.

Bleeding/Skin: I bruise and tear easily (likely related to blood thinners). Handle my skin with care and moisturise regularly.

Cognition/Communication: I live with Alzheimer’s disease. Please speak slowly, be patient, and be prepared to repeat questions. Anxiety can increase if I feel alone.

Falls/Mobility: I have limited mobility and am at risk of falls. I use a walking stick inside (sometimes I forget it), a 4WW for longer distances, and a wheelchair for extended outings.

Breathlessness: I have COPD and can become short of breath after showering or exertion.

Home environment: I have a cat in the home. Please only send workers who are comfortable with pets.

Worker preference: I prefer female support workers.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 7 October 2025

Preferred Name: Anne

Full Name: Anne Martin

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: English

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I developed this plan with my care partner and my grandson (Ioanides), who is my primary caregiver and lives with me. My son Brett was consulted as a secondary contact. This plan reflects my wishes and the information we discussed together.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I identify as an Aboriginal woman (approximately 50%) and I am part of the Stolen Generation. This history can sometimes trigger anxiety, especially fears about losing my home. Please be trauma-informed, respectful, and keep me well informed about any changes.

I value honesty, punctuality, and good communication. My family and I are “go with the flow” people—as long as we are kept informed about any changes. I have no specific religious practices and no preference about workers’ cultural backgrounds; I do prefer female workers.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I prefer female support workers who are patient, speak slowly and clearly, and are comfortable repeating information when needed.

I prefer services to occur before 2:00 PM. I appreciate punctuality and a quick call or message if a worker is running late or there is a change.

Please ensure workers are comfortable with my cat and keep doors and pathways clear.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination

My Preferred Support People

My preferred support people are my grandson (Ioanides) as my primary caregiver and my son Brett. I also value support from Mary Lou, Manet (Darren Peachy), and my health service team.

Informal Supports

I live with my grandson, who supports me day-to-day, coordinates appointments, and helps me plan my day to reduce fatigue. My son Brett also supports me, and my daughter-in-law lives 10 minutes away and can help in emergencies. My family provides transport and companionship, and helps collect my blister packs from the pharmacy.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I was born in Mildura and lived on the Murray River when I was young before being taken as part of the Stolen Generation and placed in a girls’ home in Brighton. I married young and had three children. I worked in many roles including bookbinder, cleaner, drug and alcohol counsellor, emergency housing services officer, and at sobering-up houses—giving back to the community for much of my adult life.

Interests

I like to be busy. I enjoy playing bingo at my own pace at home, gentle ball exercises, going shopping, and going out for coffee with family. I enjoy time with my family and my cat. A good day is when I have something to look forward to; a bad day is when I have back pain and feel very tired.

My Medical Information

Medical History: Alzheimer’s disease (PET-confirmed), COPD, back pain, easy bruising/skin tears, ongoing weight loss with dietitian involvement. I have been described as “frail” by my geriatrician due to tiredness and walking independence issues. I sometimes experience anxiety related to Alzheimer’s, especially if I feel alone.

Medication: Pharmacy blister packs. Panadeine Osteo two tablets in the morning and two before bed for back pain. Preventer inhaler two puffs morning and night; Ventolin as needed (often around showering). Moisturisers (e.g., QV) for skin; occasional Bepanthen or low-dose hydrocortisone on skin picking areas as directed by my GP.

Allergies: Aspirin; Norspan patches.

Mobility and Equipment: I have a walking stick (inside), a 4-wheel walker for longer distances, and a wheelchair for extended outings. I use an adjustable (hospital-style) bed and an over-bed table. I have a shower chair and stool, raised toilet seat, and handrails throughout the home. I use an “easy bar” for car transfers. I sometimes forget my stick indoors and “furniture surf.”

GP / Pharmacy: GP: Victorian Aboriginal Health Service (VAHS), South Morang (855 Plenty Road). Current GP: Dr Kieran Shields (covering while my usual GP is on maternity leave). Pharmacy: TerryWhite Chemist, Mill Park Lakes (dispenses blister packs).

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):) CALD: I am an Aboriginal woman and part of the Stolen Generation; English-speaking. Living with disability (mobility): Limited mobility; fall risk; use multiple mobility aids. Mental health: Risk of anxiety if I feel alone; risk of low mood if fatigued or in pain.

Specific Risks

Falls risk due to limited mobility and fatigue; previous slip off the bed (18 months ago) and a fall chasing my cat (2–3 years ago).

Breathlessness around showering or exertion due to COPD.

Skin tears and bruising easily; minor skin picking when bored or in sleep.

Anxiety related to Alzheimer’s, especially when I feel alone or after naps.

Occasional back pain that can limit activity and sleep.

No personal alarm currently; however, I live with family and have a grab-and-go emergency bag.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

In an emergency: Call 000. Do not perform CPR. Respect my Advance Care Directive. Then contact my family—call my grandson (primary) first, then my son Brett. If a worker arrives for a scheduled visit and cannot get a response, call my grandson first, then Brett.

Emergency preparation: I keep a medical emergency bag ready (clothing and toiletries). I have strong family support close by.

Contact details: Names and call order are documented above; specific phone numbers were discussed but not fully captured.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will shower safely and feel less breathless, with hair washed weekly and dressing supported after showers, so that I can enjoy more “good days” without feeling worn out.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I have COPD (breathless after shower), Alzheimer’s (need patience/repetition), easy bruising/skin tears, and limited mobility with falls risk.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Use my shower chair and rails; have a female support worker assist three mornings a week (Mon/Wed/Fri 10–11 AM); use Ventolin as needed before/after shower; complete the shower within ~30 minutes; weekly hair wash; dress with support; rest and hydrate after; document any breathlessness or skin issues.

Who is responsible?: I am, supported by your provider’s Personal Care workers and my grandson. When will it be done?: 3 times weekly, before 2 PM, over the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Personal Care 3 hrs/week at $85/hour ≈ 12.99 hrs/month = $1104.15/month.

Service Category: Independence Support

GOAL 2 Goal: I will keep my home clean and safe so I can move around without trip hazards and feel comfortable having visitors.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I fatigue easily and have a falls risk; I benefit from help with heavier or time-consuming tasks.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Weekly Domestic Assistance on Mondays 11 AM–12 PM for kitchen and bathroom clean, dusting, vacuum/mop of high-traffic areas, laundry/linen change as needed, and clearing walkways.

Who is responsible?: I am, supported by your provider’s Domestic Assistance worker and my grandson. When will it be done?: 1 hour weekly for the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: 1 hr/week at $85/hour ≈ 4.33 hrs/month = $368.05/month.

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 3 Goal: I will get out for coffee/shopping and meaningful activities at least 7 times per month so I feel connected and less alone.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I like to be busy but tire easily; anxiety increases if I feel alone; I need my walker or wheelchair for distance.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Social Support with a female worker on Wednesdays and Fridays 11 AM–12 PM; plan simple outings (coffee, short shop, bingo at my pace at home if I’m fatigued); use wheelchair for longer distances; pace and rest; log outings and mood.

Who is responsible?: I am, supported by your provider’s Social Support workers and my family. When will it be done?: 2 hours weekly for the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Social Support 2 hrs/week at $85/hour ≈ 8.66 hrs/month = $736.10/month, plus transport at $1.40/km (billed per actual travel).

Service Category: Independence Support

GOAL 4 Goal: I will improve my strength and balance so I can walk safely with my walker at home and reduce my risk of falls.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I have limited mobility, sometimes forget my stick, and tire easily; I have had rare falls.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Allied Health Physiotherapy 1 hour fortnightly (female physiotherapist) to review gait and balance and set a home exercise program; I will complete my prescribed exercises at least 5 days/week (10–15 minutes), and use my stick/walker consistently; workers will prompt safe technique.

Who is responsible?: I am, with your provider’s Allied Health Therapist (Physiotherapist), support workers, and my grandson. When will it be done?: Fortnightly physiotherapy over the next 12 weeks (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Physio 1 hr/fortnight at $180/hour ≈ $360/month.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 5 Goal: I will maintain comfortable feet and prevent cracked skin/tinea so walking is safer and more comfortable.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Dry, cracked skin and occasional tinea increase discomfort and falls risk; I bruise/tear easily.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Podiatry through Stellar for 1 hour every other month; follow foot care regime (moisturiser, socks/footwear guidance); workers to observe/report skin issues; keep floors clear.

Who is responsible?: I am, with your provider arranging Podiatry and my support workers. When will it be done?: One hour every other month for the next quarter (by 7 January 2026). How much will it cost?: Podiatry budgeted at $180/hour every 2 months ≈ $90/month.

Transport will be billed at $1.40/km for community outings; actual kilometers will be logged per visit and added to the above.

Care Plan Consent and Distribution

I have been involved in developing this plan and agree to the goals, services, and preferences described. I consent to share this plan with my provider, my nominated family supports (grandson and son), and my GP as needed for safe care coordination. My Advance Care Directive will be attached to my record when received.

Transcript Summary – Anne Martin (map to Standards 1–8)

Standard 1 – Consumer dignity and choice: I stated my preferences for female workers, punctuality, clear communication, and trauma-informed respect for my background as an Aboriginal woman from the Stolen Generation. I prefer services before 2 PM and want to be kept informed of any changes.

Standard 2 – Ongoing assessment and planning with consumers: My assessment covered health (Alzheimer’s, COPD, pain), mobility, equipment, home environment, risks, and social needs. My family and I co-designed goals with clear frequencies and review quarterly. My Advance Care Directive (DNR) will be attached.

Standard 3 – Personal care and clinical care: Personal Care is scheduled 3x weekly with COPD precautions. Clinical supports include physiotherapy fortnightly and podiatry bi-monthly. Allergies, skin fragility, and breathlessness were documented with mitigation strategies.

Standard 4 – Services and supports for daily living: Domestic Assistance weekly maintains a safe, clean environment. Social Support twice weekly helps me stay active and connected, including paced bingo at home or short community outings.

Standard 5 – Organisation's service environment: My home has handrails, shower chair, raised toilet seat, and a clear plan to keep pathways free of hazards. Workers will be comfortable with my cat and use safe techniques with my equipment.

Standards 6–8 – Feedback & complaints; Human resources; Organisational governance: I want honest, punctual communication. I understand how to raise concerns through my provider. Staff assigned will meet my gender preference and be trained to support dementia, COPD, and manual handling. The provider will maintain records, safeguard my Advance Care Directive, and review this plan quarterly.

Dignity of Risk Assessment (Narrative + Table)

I choose to live a full life with community outings and meaningful activities, balanced with my health conditions and risks. I accept reasonable risks (for example, going out when I may tire, showering despite possible breathlessness) and agree to mitigation strategies so I can keep doing what matters to me. These choices have been discussed with my family and care partner, and strategies are in place to reduce harm while respecting my independence and wishes.

Presence of a cat in the home I choose to keep my cat with me. Trip hazard; worker allergy risk. Advise staff in advance; keep pathways clear; close doors when moving equipment; allocate workers comfortable with pets. Agreed by me and my provider. 7 Oct 2025
Advance Care Directive – No resuscitation, no life support I choose no CPR or life support as per my Advance Care Directive. Death in the event of cardiac/respiratory arrest. saved_care_plans.html:
Care Plan

Care Alerts

I have a pacemaker (implanted last year).

I am very unsteady on my feet with a history of near-falls and one recent missed step; I am at high risk of falls due to scoliosis and a dropped foot after back surgery.

I experience severe episodic neuropathic pain (pins and needles from the waist down), rated up to 7/10, which disrupts sleep and daily function.

I have memory issues; please communicate clearly, allow time, and confirm understanding.

I have a Live Life personal alarm; my family reports I rarely use it. Please prompt me to wear it and test it.

Chlorinated pools cause skin itching; I use QV skin products after swimming.

Sweets and sugar taste bitter to me (family trait). I have no known medication allergies documented.

Emergency preference: call 000, commence resuscitation, and call my family. If there is no response at a scheduled visit, call my family first.

My Care Plan

Date of this Care Plan: 07 October 2025

Preferred Name: Greg

Full Name: Gregirious

Purpose of this Care Plan: To outline services and supports under the Support at Home Program (November 2025)

Preferred Language: Greek (I also speak English and communicate effectively)

Interpreter required?: No

People involved in developing my care plan

I participated in this assessment with my daughter Dimmy (primary contact) and my son Elias. A care partner completed the assessment with us. I agree to involve an Occupational Therapist for a mobility and home safety assessment. A professional gardener named Daniel will provide gardening services.

Things to consider about my cultural, diversity, values and belief

I was born in Greece and came to Australia in 1960. I am Greek Orthodox but I do not attend religious services. Independence and family are very important to me. I do not have any specific cultural matching requirements for care workers at this time.

My care worker, communication and service delivery preferences

I speak English as my second language and communicate well without an interpreter.

I am very unsteady; please provide close standby assistance, ensure safe transfers in and out of the car, and walk within arm’s reach, especially on stairs and wet surfaces at the pool.

Be flexible with scheduling if I have had a rough night; my family may request to delay or switch a pool visit to an at-home social activity session.

If I do not answer the door for a scheduled visit, please call my family first.

Single Provider Model: Under Support at Home, one provider manages all care coordination.

My Preferred Support People

My preferred support people are my daughter Dimmy (primary contact) and my son Elias. I also have a sister who lives nearby and close friends.

Informal Supports

My wife manages my medications and accompanies me to the pool. My family provides transport at times, supports me during outings by holding me to prevent falls, visits me regularly, and plays games (e.g., Uno) to keep me mentally stimulated.

Important things to know about me

Family Background and Life History

I am the third child in my family (two brothers and one sister). I arrived in Australia in 1960. I worked at General Motors, trained at school here, and became a bricklayer (stonemason in Greece). I later ran my own construction business building houses and commercial properties until around 1990. I have two children and several grandchildren.

Interests

A good day for me is going to the pool, seeing my grandchildren and other family, and having fewer pins and needles. I enjoy watching sports, especially soccer, and talking with friends. I used to enjoy fishing and playing backgammon but I no longer do those activities. I tend to nap during the day and benefit from more mental stimulation (e.g., playing Uno together).

My Medical Information

Medical History

I have a pacemaker (implanted last year), scoliosis, a dropped foot following a back operation, and neuropathic pain with pins and needles from the waist down. A CT scan found three collapsed ribs, which contribute to pain. I have balance issues and memory issues. I do not have documented medication allergies. Sweets and sugar taste bitter to me.

Medication

I take Lyrica (pregabalin) for nerve pain and paracetamol as needed, although these provide limited relief.

I take blood pressure medication.

I recently started mirtazapine at night to help with sleep.

My wife gives me my medications and arranges my medicines.

Mobility and Equipment

My mobility is limited. I am very unsteady and at high risk of falls. I do not currently use a walking aid; I have a brace for my foot/leg but I do not wear it regularly. I have a shower chair, raised toilet seat, handrails in the bathroom, and a recliner chair. I shower independently but need help drying my back and getting dressed after the pool.

GP / Pharmacy

My GP is Dr Lillian Risk, Donvale Medical Centre.

My pharmacy is Terry White, 274 Blackburn Road, Doncaster East.

Risk Assessment

Vulnerable Person (CALD:, Living with disability (mobility):, Mental health (low mood/isolation risk):)

CALD: Yes – I am Greek-born and English is my second language (no interpreter required).

Living with disability (mobility): Yes – high falls risk due to dropped foot and scoliosis; very unsteady on feet.

Mental health (low mood/isolation risk): Yes – I nap a lot during the day and need more stimulation; pain and poor sleep can affect my mood; I have memory issues.

Specific Risks

  • Falls risk at home, on steps, and in community settings (including wet areas at the pool).
  • Episodic severe neuropathic pain (up to 7/10) that impacts sleep and function.
  • Use of sedating medications at night (mirtazapine) may increase morning drowsiness and falls risk.
  • Skin irritation from chlorine after swimming.
  • Toe/foot problems requiring podiatry attention.
  • Pacemaker in situ – avoid strong electromagnetic fields and report any cardiac symptoms promptly.

Emergency Contacts & Instructions

Primary contact: Dimmy (daughter). Phone: 0402 201 074.

Secondary contact: Elias (son). Phone: Not documented in this transcript; this section will be updated as further details are provided.

Personal alarm: Live Life device (annual fee covered by provider). Please encourage me to wear it and test monthly.

No key lockbox at home. Family provides local support.

If I do not respond for a scheduled visit: call my family first.

Medical emergency while care is being provided: call 000, commence resuscitation, and call my family.

My Goals

GOAL 1 Goal: I will keep active and connected by going to the pool with support every Tuesday and Thursday at 9:00 AM for exercise and to see friends over the next 12 weeks, while staying safe on my feet.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I am very unsteady with a dropped foot and scoliosis; wet areas increase falls risk; chlorine causes skin itching; pain and poor sleep can make mornings difficult.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Your support worker will provide transport, walk within arm’s reach for balance, assist me to change before/after the pool, monitor for fatigue/pain, and prompt QV skin care after swimming. Sessions can be delayed or switched to an at‑home social session if I have had a rough night.

Who is responsible?: Me, my support worker, and my family. When will it be done?: 3 hours per session, twice weekly (Tuesdays and Thursdays at 9:00 AM) for 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Social Support/Transport $85/hour x 6 hours/week x 4 weeks = $2,040/month, plus $1.40/km travel (as incurred).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 2 Goal: I will reduce my risk of falls by completing an Occupational Therapy assessment and starting the recommended walking aid/home safety strategies within 8 weeks, and I will wear my foot brace whenever I leave home.

Abilities and considerations (risks): High falls risk; I have been reluctant to use aids but agree to trial a walking stick or other device; memory issues may affect carryover of strategies.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Arrange an OT home visit (up to 3 hours) to assess mobility, recommend and fit a walking aid, and advise on home modifications; practice 15 minutes of safe gait daily with the aid; family/support worker to cue brace use and safe technique.

Who is responsible?: Me, OT, support worker, and family. When will it be done?: OT visit completed within 4 weeks; aid trial and daily practice commenced by week 6; brace used on all outings by week 8. How much will it cost?: Allied Health Therapist (OT) $180/hour x up to 3 hours = up to $540 once this quarter (equipment to be funded via Support at Home equipment budget when available).

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 3 Goal: I will increase my mental stimulation by using one support session each week for social/cognitive activities at home (e.g., Uno, conversations about soccer, or visiting my sister/friends) when I cannot attend the pool, aiming to reduce daytime naps before 4 PM by 25% over 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Memory issues and variable sleep/pain; I enjoy family time, games, and sports talk which help me stay engaged.

How will we do this? (Tasks): On rough mornings, switch a scheduled pool session to an at‑home social visit; use structured activities (games, photo/music reminiscence, short walks with standby assist) and record activities completed.

Who is responsible?: Me, my support worker, and family. When will it be done?: Up to 3 hours weekly within the existing schedule over 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Reallocated within GOAL 1 Social Support/Transport hours ($0 additional per month).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 4 Goal: I will keep my garden safe and tidy to reduce outdoor trip hazards and maintain pride in my home, with Daniel (professional gardener) attending for 2 hours every 3 weeks over the next 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I am at risk of tripping on uneven pathways and overgrowth; I cannot safely perform pruning or ladder work.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Daniel will prune, tidy paths, and remove trip hazards; family and I will identify priorities before each visit.

Who is responsible?: Gardener (Daniel), me, and my family. When will it be done?: 2 hours every 3 weeks for 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Light Home & Gardening Maintenance $85/hour; approximately 2 hours every 3 weeks ≈ $227/month (average).

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 5 Goal: I will address toe discomfort and maintain healthy feet by continuing podiatry via my GP plan and, if needed, adding one in‑home top‑up podiatry visit this quarter to review nails/skin and footwear.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Overlapping toes/thick nails can cause pain and affect balance; mobility issues increase falls risk.

How will we do this? (Tasks): I will attend my usual podiatry; my GP will provide a care plan; if clinically needed, the provider will arrange one in‑home podiatry session and share advice with my family and support workers.

Who is responsible?: Me, my GP, podiatrist, and care partner. When will it be done?: Within 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Allied Health Therapist (Podiatry) $180/hour x 1 once this quarter if required (≈ $60/month averaged across the quarter). GP‑funded sessions billed separately under Medicare.

Service Category: Clinical Care

GOAL 6 Goal: I will maintain dignity and comfort overnight by using continence pads as needed (about three nights per week) with reimbursement of approximately $25/month and by tracking dry nights over the next 12 weeks.

Abilities and considerations (risks): Occasional night-time use only; need to ensure correct product and supply.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Purchase pads from the chemist; send receipts for reimbursement; review product/fit as needed.

Who is responsible?: Me and my family. When will it be done?: Ongoing over 12 weeks. How much will it cost?: Consumables reimbursement approximately $25/month.

Service Category: Everyday Living

GOAL 7 Goal: I will keep my personal alarm active and test it monthly so I can call for help if I fall or feel unwell.

Abilities and considerations (risks): I rarely use/wear the alarm despite a high falls risk.

How will we do this? (Tasks): Family will prompt me to wear the device daily; the provider will cover the annual fee; we will complete and record a monthly test call.

Who is responsible?: Me, my family, and the care partner. When will it be done?: Test monthly for the next 12 weeks (and ongoing). How much will it cost?: Annual fee approximately $70 covered by provider (≈ $6/month averaged).

Service Category: Everyday Living

Budget and Service Classifications

Service Category: Clinical Care (100% government funded) / Independence Support / Everyday Living

  • Social Support/Transport to pool and/or at-home social visits: Everyday Living – $2,040/month (6 hours/week at $85/hour) plus $1.40/km travel as incurred.
  • Light Home & Gardening Maintenance (Daniel): Everyday Living – approximately $227/month (2 hours every 3 weeks at $85/hour).
  • Occupational Therapy assessment (up to 3 hours once this quarter): Clinical Care – up to $540 once (Allied Health $180/hour).
  • Podiatry top-up (if required; one in-home session this quarter): Clinical Care – $180 once (Allied Health $180/hour), noting GP-plan sessions are billed separately.
  • Continence aids: Everyday Living – approximately $25/month (reimbursement upon receipts).
  • Personal alarm annual fee: Everyday Living – approximately $70/year (≈ $6/month averaged), covered by provider when due.

Quarterly Budget Allocation

  • Social Support/Transport: ≈ $2,040 x 3 = $6,120 (plus kilometres as incurred).
  • Gardening: ≈ $227 x 3 = $681.
  • OT assessment: up to $540 (once this quarter).
  • Podiatry top-up (if required): $180 (once this quarter).
  • Continence aids: ≈ $25 x 3 = $75.
  • Personal alarm: ≈ $6 x 3 = $18 (averaged; actual charge when renewal falls due).

Transcript Summary – Gregirious (map to Standards 1–8)

Standard 1 – Consumer dignity and choice: I stated that independence and family are important to me. I chose to continue pool visits for exercise and social connection and agreed to trial a walking aid after an OT assessment. I do not require an interpreter and have no cultural matching preferences for workers.

Standard 2 – Ongoing assessment and planning with consumers: The assessment covered my health, mobility, pain, daily living, preferences, and risks. An OT assessment (up to 3 hours) will further evaluate mobility equipment and home safety. My plan will be reviewed quarterly.

Standard 3 – Personal care and clinical care: I shower independently and need help with drying/dressing after the pool. My medications are managed by my wife; I recently started mirtazapine. Pain is managed with Lyrica and paracetamol (limited benefit). Clinical supports include OT and podiatry (as needed). My pacemaker is noted.

Standard 5 – Organisation's service environment: Workers will provide close standby assistance for mobility and safe transfers, especially around wet areas, and follow my communication preferences. If I do not respond at a visit, family will be contacted first.

I agree to trial a walking aid and to wear my foot brace when I go out. I know that sedating medicines and poor sleep may increase my falls risk in the morning; on such days I may switch a pool session to an at‑home social visit. I acknowledge my personal alarm helps me call for assistance and agree to wear and test it regularly.
